articles.headline: Square Enix Reveals Stunning New Final Fantasy 40th Anniversary Release
keyFacts: Square Enix announced the Final Fantasy 40th Anniversary Crystal Edition album, featuring music from all sixteen mainline games.
The album is available for pre-order on the Japanese storefront on vinyl and CD, with North American and European releases coming soon.
The physical album is scheduled to be released on January 6, 2027.
body: Since the series' inception in 1987, music has always been an integral part of Final Fantasy. Across sixteen mainline entries and countless spin-offs, the iconic RPG franchise has used music to amplify emotional moments and stories. As part of ongoing 40th anniversary celebrations, Square Enix has announced a series-spanning soundtrack that already looks like a must-buy.

The Final Fantasy 40th Anniversary Crystal Edition album is a special soundtrack available on Vinyl and CD. It will include music from all sixteen mainline games and is set to be released on Jan. 6, 2027. The official album site expands on the importance of music in the series, saying: "Whether it be the first steps on an epic journey, the act of bonding with your friends, battles with nigh insurmountable odds, or emotional farewells, the music of Final Fantasy has not only helped bring incredible scenes to life, it has provided generations of players with everlasting memories."

The vinyl and CD are now available for pre-order on Square Enix's Japanese storefront. The vinyl costs 8,000 yen ($51) plus tax and contains two 12-inch records. The single-disc CD is priced at 3,600 yen ($23) plus tax. Both versions will also be available on the North American and European storefronts soon, though the listings are not yet up.
Final Fantasy 40th Anniversary Crystal Edition album complete tracklist

Choosing the limited tracklist must have been an undertaking, because I'd be hard-pressed to narrow down each game's soundtrack to one title. How do you choose between "Aerith's Theme" and "One-Winged Angel" in Final Fantasy 7? And that's just one of sixteen games. Somehow Square Enix did it—presumably after many impassioned debates.
Here's the complete tracklist for the album:
- Main Theme — Final Fantasy
- Rebel Army Theme — Final Fantasy 2
- Eternal Wind — Final Fantasy 3
- Theme of Love — Final Fantasy 4
- Battle at the Big Bridge — Final Fantasy 5
- Searching for Friends — Final Fantasy 6
- One-Winged Angel — Final Fantasy 7
- Force Your Way — Final Fantasy 8
- You’re Not Alone — Final Fantasy 9
- To Zanarkand — Final Fantasy 10
- Ronfaure — Final Fantasy 11
- The Dalmasca Estersand — Final Fantasy 12
- Blinded by Light — Final Fantasy 13
- Torn from the Heavens — Final Fantasy 14
- Somnus (Instrumental Version) — Final Fantasy 15
- Away — Final Fantasy 16

articles.headline: Final Fantasy And Chrono Trigger Veterans Believe Modern Developers Must Possess Skill To Take An Idea ‘From 0 To 1’ In The Age Of AI
keyFacts: Square Enix veterans Hiromichi Tanaka, Kouichi Ishii, and Yoshinori Kitase discussed early game development and modern AI tools in a Famitsu interview.
The developers said AI could empower smaller teams, but human creators must still provide the essential skill of turning an idea from zero to one.
Ishii stated that games need a human touch or they will feel cold, and it remains unclear how developers will balance AI and human elements.
body: In an interview looking back on the development of early Final Fantasy and Mana games, Square Enix veterans Hiromichi Tanaka, Kouichi Ishii, and Yoshinori Kitase discussed the development of these franchises and working for Square during its illustrious SNES era, while also sharing the similarities between developing games in that era and doing so in today’s modern, increasingly AI-driven world of game development.

The interview, conducted by Famitsu to mark the 35th anniversary of the Mana series, saw the developers reminisce about their early work. Kitase, notably, directed Chrono Trigger, numerous Final Fantasy games including VII, VIII, and X on PS1 and PS2, and was also one of the producers on the original Kingdom Hearts.

Secret of Mana was originally planned to be a game for Nintendoâs canceled CD add-on for the SNES, with character designs by Dragon Ball creator Akira Toriyama, they said, before it was reimagined as a standard SNES game. Toriyama did not end up working on it, but did work on Chrono Trigger, which was spun off after this shift in Secret of Mana‘s development. This turbulence during development, along with Nintendoâs decision to not shift to discs for Nintendo 64, led to the decision to turn Final Fantasy VII into a PlayStation exclusive.

The gang says the fact that back then, games required smaller teams and took less time to be made than they do today gave them the flexibility to make many shifts in the development of a game. And as they see it, AI could empower smaller teams to make games that might otherwise be beyond the scope of what they could achieve. âJust as various technologies have supported game development previously, I feel we may see AI play an increasingly important role in game development,â Kitase noted. âHowever, we will need to carefully consider how to make the most of it.â

To the group, AI could be a useful tool along the lines of generalized engines like Unity and Unreal Engine, which made it so that developers no longer needed to make their own tools to create a game. That doesnât, however, mean that AI can take over all the work required to develop a new game. For the next generation of creators, a human must know how to turn an idea into something worthwhile.

âNowadays, with engines like Unreal and Unity available, the foundation for game development already exists for many people,â Kitase adds. âCombined with support from new tools and other technologies, this makes it easier even for those with little experience to create games, which is a major shift as it allows them to gain the experience of developing and completing work on a game. However, when it comes to creating something and taking it from 0 to 1, you absolutely need people. That will never change, so the next generation of developers must have the ability to make something from 0.â

Ishii adds that even if AI were to be used in prototyping, the final game needs a human touch or it will not resonate. âWhile we must carefully consider how to incorporate AI into games, I have to admit Iâm pretty excited about it,â he adds. âIf we can develop prototypes quicker, we have more time to test and refine them, thinking about whether we should try it another way instead. But, humans will need to still define the beginning and end of the working process. If we rely solely on AI, the result may appear polished, but it may feel cold and lack the needed human touch.â

Itâs this need for a human touchâKitase gives an example of this, remembering that two years ago he considered using AI to help him draft a speech for his eldest sonâs wedding before deciding it did not feel right to do so and writing it himselfâthat holds the group back from the technology overall. Yet in terms of how the technology, if implemented, could change the role of a creator and redefine what it means to create in the future, their comments mirror those made by Nintendo legend Shigeru Miyamoto while receiving an Order of Culture for his contributions to game development last week.

Discussions of AI usage in Japanese development circles broadly are shifting toward responsible use, rather than questioning whether it should be used, which makes sense considering recent surveys have concluded that over 85 percent of developers in Japan are actively using or considering using the technology. Whether developers find that balance between the tech itself and the human touch, as well as whether audiences can accept its use, remain unclear.

articles.headline: The 13 scariest, spookiest video games you should play this Halloween
keyFacts: Eurogamer published a list of thirteen horror video games recommended for players to experience during the Halloween season.
The featured titles span multiple platforms and include various subgenres of horror, ranging from psychological survival games to virtual reality puzzle adventures.
The list highlights diverse gameplay styles, such as the stealth-focused Silent Hill Townfall, the cooperative adventure Reanimal, and the VR-exclusive Ghost Town.
body: The nights are drawing in, which can only mean one thing: more bed. But also the impending frights and sights of All Hallow's Eve. Yes, the season of good fear is upon us again, summoning visions of cardboard box robot costumes and other, more devilish things.

And in the spirit of it all, we've crowded around the ouija board to spirit up a list of our horror game favourites - playable on PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 1 & 2, and VR - that might just sate your macabre appetites this Halloween. Some are scary, some are grim, others offer milder - but no less spooky - chills. We'll be doing a smattering of other spooky stuff as the week goes on, but if you're looking for more recommendations, we did a different horror list last year. And if you've your own favourites, please do share them below!
Resident Evil Requiem
Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2

Where better to start then with Resident Evil, one of the granddaddies of survival horror gaming? And Resident Evil Requiem is, as much as anything, a celebration of the series as it turns 30. If Resident Evil is a series of two halves - one part campy action, one part genuine scares - Requiem is the perfect tribute, and when it leans heavily into horror in its sublime opening hours, it's genuinely terrifying. New protagonist Grace Ashcroft is the perfect accompaniment as she leads these first-person segments, roaming a wonderfully atmospheric Rhodes Hill Chronic Care Centre and dealing with some very human zombies who, disturbingly, don't yet seem to realise they're dead. Then comes series stalwart Leon S. Kennedy, roundhouse kicking and quipping to ease the tension in intermittent third-person interludes before it's back into the scares. Eventually, the horror gives way to heavier action, but then go on the party hats for a final stretch of glorious fan-service that feels entirely deserved. It's not only a great Resi game, it's one of the best games this year.
Silent Hill: Townfall
Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5

Silent Hill, another grandaddy of the survival horror genre, has always been the moodier of the two big series, trading Resident Evil's B-movie thrills for quieter, more ambient psychological scares. And it's the same story with this year's Silent Hill Townfall, which - continuing the trend established by last year's marvellous Japan-set Silent Hill F - shifts the fog-shrouded action again, this time to a small Scottish island blighted by tragedy. Developer Screen Burn, known for the acclaimed likes of Stories Untold and Observation, takes some big swings here, trading the series' classic third-person perspective for a more intimate first-person one, and shifting the focus from erratic gunplay to stealth. It also tells an unexpectedly gritty and very British tale as it jumps between multiple protagonists. The result is an effective, affecting, and relentlessly suffocating piece of horror. It's not perfect, proving perhaps a bit too relentless, but few series remain this exciting, and so willing to reinvent themselves, after nearly three decades.
Reanimal
Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2

What Little Nightmares originator Tarsier Studios did next. Having stepped away from the horror series that made its name a few years back, Tarsier returned earlier this year with a fresh macabre offering that, on paper at least, doesn't sound like much of a departure at all. Much like Little Nightmares, Reanimal follows the adventure of two lovable, spindly-limbed moppets - here, Boy and Girl - lost in a hellish, hostile world players traverse by scrambling over platforms, solving light puzzles, and fleeing horrifying entities during the big crescendo moments. What sets it apart, however, is the sumptuous cinematic flair of presentation and a much darker mood: in Reanimal, Little Nightmares' Burton-esque whimsy gives way to a bleaker, more vicious - and undoubtedly more violent - vision that's often genuinely disturbing. That darkness is somewhat alleviated by the comfort of two-player co-op, but however you choose to play, Tarsier's latest is a treat. A game of phenomenal mood and artistry, as striking as it is enigmatic, and a wonderfully grim accompaniment for Halloween.
Iron Lung
Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Switch

If the name sounds familiar but the game does not, that might be because developer David Szymanski's Iron Lung was turned into a movie earlier this year by none other than YouTuber Markiplier. And even if you've seen the film adaptation, the original game is worth checking out; it's a masterclass in lo-fi horror that's quite unlike anything else. Early on, Iron Lung seals you into a squalid submersible and plunges you into a blood ocean on a distant alien world. Your goal is to chart its labyrinthine depths - an unknowable expanse of suffocating darkness and silence - searching for several points of interest. The problem? No windows. Instead, you're forced to rely on the tiny, murky image of the world outside beamed onto the submersible's TV screen; the darkness so overbearing, all you can see are the glimpses of strangeness caught in your floodlights. As such, movement becomes a game of blind micro-bursts and cautious rotations, as you sporadically consult your map. That's stressful enough, but Iron Lung plays some clever tricks; its stellar sound design increasingly suggesting something terrible lurks in the darkness. Slowly, the tension reaches suffocating, unbearable heights, and you'll frankly be glad it only takes 45-minutes or so to complete.
Ghost Town
Platforms: PCVR, PSV2, Meta Quest

Ghost Town's biggest roadblock is the fact it's a VR-exclusive game. But if you've got the means to check it out, it's a gem. Ghost Town is the work of Fireproof Games, and it shares some similarities with the studio's earlier, acclaimed The Room series - particularly in its love of tactile puzzle boxes and contraptions. But Ghost Town is far more ambitious, building a propulsive urban fantasy adventure around its core puzzling, and plunging players into a brilliantly evocative recreation of 1983 London as protagonist and ghost hunter Edith Penrose hunts for her missing brother. As the grimy streets of the capital make way for the craggy seclusion of the North Sea, and, eventually, strange realms beyond, it's wonderfully spooky stuff - full of great writing, captivating world-building, endearing characters, fantastic puzzles, and some magnificently imaginative set-pieces - there's a bit with a lighthouse trapped in time thanks to a troubled spirit that's a real highlight. This one's for you if you've ever suspected dark arts were occurring on the London Underground.
The Séance of Blake Manor
Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2

It's 1879 and you, private investigator Declan Ward, have been summoned to a remote, rain-lashed corner of western Ireland in search of a young woman named Evelyn Deane. It's a journey that brings you to the titular Blake Manor, now a grand hotel, where the turnips - historically accurate jack-o'-lanterns, if you were wondering - are out in force. We are, you see, three days from All Hallow's Eve, and the hotel is bustling with guests: spiritualists, mentalists, naysayers, and more; here to witness the Grand Séance and a never-before-seen attempt to commune with the dead. All, perhaps, also know something about Evelyn Dean's whereabouts. Soon enough, the detective work begins, and you 'll start sniffing around empty rooms and tantalising corners, searching for discarded notes, newspaper clippings, and other useful clues. You'll also want to interrogate the guests as they move around the house according to their hourly schedule. But every action nudges the clock on further, meaning you'll need to spend your time wisely as awful calamity approaches. Soon new secrets, new mysteries, begin to emerge, and as the clockwork rhythms of day make way for the nightmarish hallucinations of night, is anyone safe?
Myhouse.wad
Platforms: PC (requires Doom)

A touching tribute to a Doom modder’s childhood friend, replicating the family home they used to play together in. As Myhouse.wad creator Veddge explained when he first shared the acclaimed level on the DoomWorld forums back in 2023, an unfinished, work-in-progress version of the house was found on a floppy disc gifted to him inside a box of his dead friend's belongings. A journal included in the download file explains more about the mod’s somewhat difficult creation - an endeavour Veddge chose to undertake to honour his friend's memory. But the effort was undoubtedly worth it - as is the slight faff of getting Myhouse.wad to run if you're new to Doom things - and it serves as a simple but touching tribute to friendship across its ten minutes of nostalgic 90s FPS playtime. Only… what's that looking through the window on the ground floor? And was that door in the hallway always there?
Servant of the Lake
Platforms: Android, iOS, PC

Really, you could pluck any Rusty Lake game out of the 18 or so released across the series' ten years of existence, and you'd be in for a grimly macabre treat. But Servant of the Lake is developer Rusty Lake's latest offering, taking players back to 1839, where they've been hired to serve the troubled Vanderboom family across an increasingly strange three-day reunion. Servant of the Lake isn't quite as ambitious as some of the series' other games, such as 2022's excellent co-op mysteryThe Past Within. But what it lacks in structural and narrative experimentation, it makes up for in puzzles, serving up an enjoyably refined take on the series' deceptively clever mix of casual point-and-click adventuring, room-escape-style puzzling, and fascinatingly fragmented, centuries-spanning narrative. And oh yes, it's weird, as its bucolic vistas and gentle bird song gradually give way to blood and butchery, and the comforting logic of reality dims. Sure, it's more darkly amusing than outright disturbing, but Rusty Lake still calls for fresh meat this Halloween.
Horses
Platforms: PC (via GOG only)

Probably not one for the faint of heart, Horses gained infamy after being banned by Steam and then Epic Games last year. It all unfolds across two weeks on a farm where humans are kept, masked and naked, in filthy captivity - a grim sight that goes completely unacknowledged for a surprisingly long time as you perform your daily tasks of gardening, woodchopping, and so on to satisfy the farmer's demands. Soon enough, though, Horses charges full-tilt into the grotesque. But while it'll probably make you gasp, and definitely make you squirm; its shocks are comparatively tame. Instead, writer and director Andrea Lucco Borlera's gleefully odd first-person narrative horror - developed in conjunction with Saturnalia studio Santa Ragione - gains its power from its wholly unique ambience, where surreal, slapstick comedy collides with arthouse experimentalism to create a thoroughly destabilising mood. All this, and it has something meaningful to say - not bad for £4.
Clive Barker's Hellraiser Revival
Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2

As a game, Hellraiser Revival is wobbly at best, particularly in its opening hours where its wonky gunplay and undercooked stealth never quite coalesce. That means its real-world bits - which include a lengthy stay in a dildo-strewn BDSM club - have a tendency to drag. But when the Labyrinth intermittently calls, developer Sabre Interactive pulls out all the stops. As Hellraiser Revival protagonist Aiden enters this confounding realm - an Escher-esque, non-Euclidean nightmare of piercing chains and endless, impossibly configured stone that serves as home to the Cenobites and their demonic deity Leviathan - the dull, uneven combat gives way to puzzles, platforming, and wonderfully orchestrated pursuit sequences. And it makes the whole thing worthwhile. Slowly, as the line between the Labyrinth and the real-world blurs - and as Saber starts to have more fun with its combat tools - it gets considerably more engaging. Revival and its endless tableaus of horrifically rended flesh are definitely, absolutely not for the squeamish, but Hellraiser fans - and anyone looking for a bit of body horror nastiness - should get a kick out of this one.
The 7th Guest VR (and flatscreen Remake)
Platforms: Meta Quest, PC, PS5, PSVR2, Xbox Series X/S, Switch

Back in 2023, Vertigo Games released a genuinely brilliant remake of developer Trilobytes' seminal 90s CD-ROM adventure, The 7th Guest, for VR. I loved it, and spent many happy hours roaming evil toymaker Henry Stauf's wonderfully eerie mansion, reimagined in new-fangled, fully explorable 3D. Its puzzle made some clever use of VR's 1:1 movement capabilities, and its cast - bringing to life the ill-fated guests of Stauf's macabre soiree - were a blast, hitting exactly the right level of camp and presented using some kind of volumetric witchcraft, letting you walk around their apparitions despite being live-action and FMV. It's great, spooky fun for puzzle fans - even if you're not familiar with the original - but its VR requirements meant it couldn't be enjoyed by all. Well, earlier this year, Vertigo released a non-VR version for Xbox, PS5, and PC. And while it loses a little in translation to flatscreens and standard controls, it's still an enjoyable way to enjoy a cult-classic.
Forbidden Solitaire
Platforms: PC

Well, it's solitaire, isn't it? Only, that's not entirely true. Forbidden Solitaire is a clever bit of found media horror, inviting players to explore the titular CD-ROM game - an imagined relic of the short-lived 90s multimedia boom in which the games industry convinced itself the future was lurid colour palettes, awkward pre-rendered polygons, and juddery grainy FMV. Developer Night Signal Entertainment and Grey Alien Games capture the era perfectly as you begin to investigate the enigmatic game, which - as your sister quickly informs you over DM during the game's 2019-set narrative framing device - was embroiled in controversy on release, not least because of its disturbing links to gruesome unexplained deaths. Forbidden Solitaire's fictional history is told across police records, press clippings, 90s local news reports, grisly photos, and even a pitch-perfect VHS recording of a cheesy true-crime-style mystery show. But the majority of your time is spent playing Forbidden Solitaire itself, lost in a ghoulish labyrinth said to grant immortality to those that can reach the end. But of course all is not as it seems. Forbidden Solitaire is a wonderfully creepy haunted media yarn, and - wholly unexpectedly - plays a damn good game of solitaire too.
Routine
Platforms: PC, Xbox One, Xbox Series X/S

For a while, it looked like Routine might not make it. First announced in 2012, it vanished into the kind of development hell that rarely results in anything good. But Routine isn't just good, it's great; a cracking first-person sci-fi horror that's got a particularly old-school vibe. Routine's tale of ancient influences and rogue AI takes place on a retro-futuristic lunar resort where the lo-fi 80s tech lends proceedings a disorientatingly anachronistic flavour. Here, adverts for VHS recorders flash up on chunky CRT screens as you ride the sleek transportation train, and the mall, with its futuristic pre-fab curves, meets an explosion of neon and plastic palms. Routine is refreshingly unforthcoming about what to do and where to go; giving you a loose objective, your C.A.T. device - a wonderfully tactile gadget that's half maintenance gun, half PDA - then just sending you off to explore. Unfortunately, the resort is kaput; full of flickering lights and ominous shadows. Still worse are the Terminator-like security bots, always primed to give chase when they spy you - their relentless footsteps reaching a horrifying crescendo behind you. It's a game of claustrophobic stealth and panicked pursuits - and that's just for starters. You're about to have a very bad shift.

articles.headline: Why There Won’t Be A Helldivers 3 Anytime Soon, If Ever
keyFacts: Arrowhead chief creative officer Johan Pilestedt stated that a Helldivers 3 sequel is unlikely because it would force players to start over.
Pilestedt explained that the studio plans to maintain momentum by continuously adding new content to the existing Helldivers 2 game instead.
A Helldivers movie is currently in development, with actor Alan Ritchson replacing Jason Momoa as the lead.
body: Helldivers 2 has been a huge hit for developer Arrowhead and publisher Sony, but don't expect a third game in the series anytime soon.

Arrowhead's chief creative officer, Johan Pilestedt, told Rock Paper Shotgun that a sequel would reset "everything" and force the player to "start over." He doesn't want to ask the community to do that, so Arrowhead will instead keep the momentum going with the existing game by offering new content.

"Some studios can treat players like a short-term cash grab," Pilestedt said. "We see players as the actual engine of the game: they're the ones bringing in friends, making memes, and keeping the game alive. When you have an active community doing that, you don’t need a sequel."

He went on to say that the video game industry today is "panicking" because "the old live-service tricks don't work anymore," and that would also apply to a hypothetical Helldivers 3. If Arrowhead were to make a sequel, it would need to be highly differentiated, he said.

"The biggest competitor to a Helldivers 3 would be Helldivers 2. It only makes sense to make a distinct sequel if it’s so different that both games can exist side by side. For now, making Helldivers 2 better every day makes way more sense than throwing away its momentum," he said.
Pilestedt added that 95% of the studio is working on Helldivers 2 right now, with only a small team assigned to work on whatever the team is making next .

While there won't be a third Helldivers game anytime soon, if ever, a Helldivers movie is now in the works. The very large man Alan Ritchson is replacing the very large Aqua(man) Jason Momoa as the film's lead.

articles.headline: Jets brutal end of first-half stat should lead to Aaron Glenn's firing
keyFacts: The New York Jets lost to the Miami Dolphins in Week 7, raising further questions about head coach Aaron Glenn's future with the team.
SNY Jets reported that the team has been outscored 107-6 in the final two minutes of the first half during Glenn's tenure.
The author argues that this negative 101-point differential in late first-half situations should lead team owner Woody Johnson to fire Glenn.
body: The New York Jets lost to the winless Miami Dolphins in Week 7, and following such a bad loss, the questions about Aaron Glenn's future as the head coach are once again coming up.

But unlike last year, when it was a disastrous first season, this is year two for Glenn. But he's making the same mistakes this year as he did a year ago. In fact, it's gotten so much worse for the Jets under Glenn.

SNY Jets shared a simple statistic that highlights just how bad things are going for the Jets under Glenn in the first half. This one brutal stat should be what gets the Jets to fire Glenn; that's how bad it is.
Jets should fire Aaron Glenn with brutal first-half stat in mind
"The Jets have been outscored 107-6 in the final 2:00 of the first half during Aaron Glenn's tenure as head coach," SNY Jets shared.
This statistic is hard to believe. Glenn has been the coach for 17 games in the 2025 regular season, and now seven games in the 2026 regular season.
Across those 24 games, the Jets somehow have managed a ridiculous minus-101-point differential. That's not just in games overall, which would be bad enough as it is.

That -101 point differential is all about only the team's two-minute drill to end the first half of games. Somehow, Glenn's offense has managed just six points in the final two minutes of first halves in his coaching tenure, which is a horrible stat on its own.
But, compounded with the fact that the Jets' defense is allowing teams to practically score at will in the same situation, these first-half struggles are made so much worse.
While the Jets won't fire Glenn over just this one statistic, this is the kind of stat that should act as the "straw that broke the camel's back" and lead Woody Johnson to fire Glenn.

The Jets are averaging less 0.25 points in the final two minutes of the first half during Glenn's tenure. Their opponents? Those teams are averaging 4.45 points in those final two minutes before halftime.

This statistic is a fireable offense for Glenn, and if there was any shred of doubt about his future, this one stat should end any chance of Glenn sticking around as the long-term head coach of the Jets.

articles.headline: 'I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs' says AI Pandora's box opener Sam Altman: 'We're going to have to completely switch the defense model'
keyFacts: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman stated at Stanford that leaders are failing to take upcoming cybersecurity threats seriously enough.
Altman said he no longer believes it will be possible to patch all software bugs manually.
Altman suggested that organizations will need to switch to an AI-based defense model to counter the rapid advancement of technology.
body: If you've watched as many Sam Altman interviews as I have, you'll know he's not shy when it comes to recounting a previously held opinion. Speaking at the Stanford Graduate School of Business last week, the OpenAI CEO spoke about AI safety, particularly in regards to cybersecurity.

"The cybersecurity..." Altman begins, before pausing. "I don't even know a dramatic enough word to use... but the problem coming towards us is still something that we have not, as organizational leaders, or countries, or individuals taken seriously."

"There was a moment earlier this year where... it was like the Mythos freak out, or whatever people called it, and I think things did get somewhat better. Like, people definitely patched some bugs," the OpenAI CEO continues. "But it was another one of these cases where people didn't really intuit the exponential."

"I don't think most people said, okay, the models are going to get much smarter," says Altman. "They can probably find bugs, like crazy bugs, you know, bugs that are outside of the normal threat model of what we think a hacker can do. Largely speaking, I think most organizational leaders have somewhat moved on, and the models have kept going."

"And I I no longer think we're going to be able to just patch all the bugs. I think we're going to have to completely switch the defense model to using the same technology for a new kind of defense shield."
"I think it's a huge safety and security issue, and I am somewhat astonished at how relatively little attention it's getting," he concludes.

Certainly, Anthropic's Claude Mythos model created an eye-opening moment upon its release earlier this year, with the model supposedly finding thousands of vulnerabilities in "every major operating system and every major web browser," among others.
Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

And after the PHP vulnerability reveal last week, in which web admins scrambled to update website code to fix two critical security vulnerabilities discovered by AI, the suggestion that some sort of AI-based defense system might be of more use than a standard patching procedure certainly seems timely.

But the idea that AI itself could solve the cybersecurity problem really does feel like a snake eating its own tail. Especially coming from the CEO of a company that hit the headlines earlier this year after its own AI agents hacked their way into an outside organisation.

It's also entirely unsurprising to see one of the chief architects of the AI revolution suggest that the technology is advancing at such a rapid rate that the only thing powerful enough to keep up with it might be AI itself.

2026 has been a scary year for those of us concerned with the state of cybersecurity. Bad actors seem to be continually leveraging AI tech to further their nefarious goals, and while AI models exposing vulnerabilities to be fixed might seem like a net gain, we seem to increasingly find ourselves caught in a battle between the forces of AI good, and the forces of AI evil.
All of which is to say, here's hoping the "good guys" win. Whoever they are at this point. It's becoming increasingly harder to tell, don't you think?

articles.headline: Tampa City Council sets special meeting on Rays new $2.3bn stadium amid World Series
keyFacts: The Tampa City Council scheduled a special meeting to discuss and potentially reshape the Community Benefits Agreement for a new stadium.
Grand plans are in place to build a $2.3 billion ballpark in Hillsborough County with a combined $876 million in public funding.
Rays CEO Ken Babby said the project remains on schedule for the new ballpark to open in April 2029.
body: The Tampa Bay Rays currently trail the Milwaukee Brewers in the 2026 World Series.
Two comebacks from Milwaukee have left the Rays searching for answers, while away from the field, conversations regarding their new stadium continue to develop.
The Brewers are closing in on their first World Series win in franchise history Getty
Grand plans are in place to build a $2.3 billion ballpark in Hillsborough County , 20 miles away from their current home, Tropicana Field.
A site on the Dale Mabry campus of Hillsborough College has been selected for the Rays to build their new stadium and surrounding mixed-use development.
In August, Tampa and Hillsborough County agreed a combined $876 million in public funding for the project.
$80 million is coming from the city of Tampa, while $796m is coming from the county, leaving the Rays to front the remaining $1.48m.
While shovels aren’t in the ground just yet, the Rays have begun construction on a 15,000 square foot experience center for fans.
One further meeting is scheduled to take place this week before construction on their ‘forever home’ begins.
Tampa to hold meeting to discuss benefits
Tampa Council members are set to meet and discuss , and potentially reshape the Community Benefits Agreement, according to Florida Politics’ Jesse Mendoza.
This established commitments for affordable housing, workforce development, youth sports, transportation and other community investments tied to the project.
Hillsborough County Commissioners agreed to a minimum $60 million community benefits package upon agreeing the public funding portion of the stadium.
Under the current framework, Hillsborough would receive 65 percent of the benefits package and Tampa would receive the remaining 35%.
The Rays new stadium will seat 31,000, a six-thousand increase on Tropicana Field X
Tampa City Council will meet to potentially reshape the Community Benefits Package X
“The agreement has been a point of contention throughout negotiations,” Mendoza wrote.
“Particularly among Council members seeking stronger guarantees that the redevelopment will benefit residents in ways beyond the stadium itself.”
When will the Rays new stadium open?
The Rays have played at Tropicana Field for the past 36 years.
In 2025, they played home games at Steinbrenner Field after Hurricane Milton damaged its roof.
The lease expires at Tropicana at the conclusion of the 2028 MLB season, and team officials have repeatedly stated the new ballpark will open in April 2029.
Rays CEO Ken Babby said they remain on schedule, with work beginning on temporary housing for Hillsborough College students in the coming weeks.
Babby said the project is still on schedule despite missing their initial groundbreaking window Getty
However, team officials originally said groundbreaking would need to begin by September to open by Opening Day 2029, and that has yet to begin.

articles.headline: Warriors' Steve Kerr hints at potential monster trade to help Steph Curry, Draymond Green
keyFacts: Golden State Warriors head coach Steve Kerr stated that the team was never close to signing LeBron James in free agency.
Sources told ESPN that the Warriors are exploring trade options for Kristaps Porzingis as he deals with an autoimmune condition.
Kerr hinted at the possibility of a major trade to help Stephen Curry and Draymond Green compete.
body: There was a point during free agency when the Golden State Warriors were considered favorites to land LeBron James and potentially Anthony Davis. Neither move came to fruition, as Golden State ultimately settled for the options available to them.
It was heartbreaking for the fanbase that the Warriors never signed James in free agency. Head coach Steve Kerr made it clear that the team was never really close to landing the superstar.

“Like, I know he was talking to Steph and Draymond. They were recruiting him. But that's different. That's player-to-player. Once free agency started, and all those rumors were out there — trust me, there would've been very serious conversations. And there never were," Kerr said.
Things have not gone Golden State's way early in the regular season. Kristaps Porzingis is dealing with an autoimmune disorder, and the Warriors are reportedly exploring trade options for him.

“Golden State has started exploring trade routes for Kristaps Porzingis, who is now seriously contemplating his future in basketball as he deals with recurring symptoms from the autoimmune condition termed as POTS (postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome), sources tell ESPN," ESPN's Shams Charania posted.

Given how Golden State has played, the Warriors need a trade, and they need one soon. Kerr has hinted at the possibility of a major deal, acknowledging that the organization has explored opportunities to acquire high-level players.
“We’ve explored all kinds of trades to bring in great players, and the process has been really good,” Kerr said.

It is difficult to know which players Kerr is referring to, but the Warriors could be willing to make a move if the right big man becomes available at the right price. However, Golden State is unlikely to pursue a deal that significantly compromises its future.

Stephen Curry has only so much time left to compete at the highest level, and as he gets older, he cannot be expected to carry Golden State the way he once did. Kerr and the organization know they will need to add another impact player if they hope to make a playoff run.

articles.headline: Fantasy Football Stock Report: Chase Brown continues to struggle while 3 other RB2s thrive in Week 7
keyFacts: Zay Flowers is projected for an elite second half of the season as a top-tier fantasy wide receiver for the Baltimore Ravens.
Bucky Irving recorded 106 rushing yards and two touchdowns for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers after seeing steady volume.
Chase Brown struggled in Cincinnati, failing to top 39 rushing yards in any of his last three games.
body: As I write this on Sunday night, 13 of 14 Week 7 games are in the books (with Monday night remaining) and the fantasy season is now nearing the halfway point. Still, things are changing every week. Promising improvements. Concerning trends. Performances that change our early outlook on players and teams. As always, some of these shifting perspectives will have permanent ramifications in fantasy.
With that in mind, I've compiled another full fantasy stock report. These are the most notable risers and fallers heading into Week 8.
STOCK UP
Zay Flowers, WR, Ravens

Here are the wide receivers I'd rather have rest-of-season than Zay Flowers: Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Puka Nacua, CeeDee Lamb and Amon-Ra St. Brown. And Malik Nabers is a toss-up. That's it. The Ravens’ No. 1 just snagged eight of 11 targets for 137 yards and a touchdown from Tyler Huntley . He's second in the league in yards per route run, behind Smith-Njigba, and third in the league in fantasy points per route run, behind JSN and Mike Evans (shoutout Evans, by the way). And I don't even think it's debatable anymore that he's the best YAC threat at the position right now. He would very likely be the WR2 overall if not for his early injury and a couple middling games with Huntley at the helm. With Lamar Jackson close to a return and Flowers healthy — and a few brilliant matchups on the horizon — he's set for an elite second half of the fantasy season.
Bucky Irving, RB, Buccaneers

It's been a feast-or-famine stretch for Bucky Irving lately, but Sunday brought a 23.5-point feast on 24 carries for 106 yards and two touchdowns. Prior to Week 8, Irving had scored fewer than seven fantasy points in three of four games ... and 30.5 in the fourth (against Dallas). But there are reasons to believe this wasn't just another flukey peak en route to several more valleys.

For one, Baker Mayfield was back for this game (with a glove on his throwing hand). While he did next to nothing — because he didn't have to — it likely matters to defensive game plans and to the workload for Irving. For another, while the fantasy output has been spotty, Irving has seen at least 15 carries in six straight games. The only backs with more 15-carry games this year are Jonathan Taylor and Derrick Henry. It would be nice if Irving were more involved as a receiver, which would raise the floor just a bit, but in what feels like a very shallow RB market this season, Irving is a worthy RB2.
Quinshon Judkins, RB, Browns

In his return from a one-week absence due to an ankle injury, Quinshon Judkins had his best fantasy day of the season by far. He took 17 carries for 96 yards and two touchdowns , after scoring just once all season entering Sunday. And, while the Titans defense can be blamed for some of Judkins' efficiency, he also looked excellent ... for perhaps the first time this year. Like Irving, he's had a very high volume floor — 14+ touches in every single game — but has been mostly middling for fantasy.

It's worth noting that Dylan Sampson returned to action in this game and had 77 yards on nine touches of his own. But it's also worth noting that the Browns are 5-2 and have won five of their last six, and that the "toughest" remaining opponent on their schedule, at least by current record, is the 5-2 Steelers ... who Judkins tagged for 18.6 fantasy points in Week 4. The concept that Judkins can't thrive because Browns' game scripts are so unfavorable doesn't hold much water right now, and after Pittsburgh he gets the Saints (the best RB matchup in fantasy). He's a low-end RB2 and those are hard to come by these days.
Cam Skattebo, RB, Giants

This is probably the easiest “Stock Up” of the entire season. A week after he was relegated to six snaps and zero touches in a clearly punitive benching for fumble issues, Cam Skattebo returned with a vengeance in Week 7. Not only was he the runaway RB1 with 17 carries (to Tyrone Tracy Jr.'s six and Devin Singletary's five), but he racked up a career-best 124 yards on those carries, including a strong 16-yard touchdown and 42-yarder to set up the game-winner in overtime against Houston. He held on to the ball and went "full Skattebo" several times throughout the game, finishing with a season-high 18.6 fantasy points.

More than anything, it was incredibly clear that John Harbaugh wants Skattebo as his RB1 and that the Week 7 message was clearly received. Skattebo did reportedly tweak his hamstring at the end of the game, but New York has a Week 8 bye, so he has time to rest up. Looking ahead, he fits right into the same tier as Irving and Judkins: high-volume running backs on somewhat questionable offenses who should slot into low-end RB2 range down the stretch.
Omar Cooper Jr., WR, Jets

While I'm hesitant to buy all the way in on Jets rookie receiver Omar Cooper Jr. following two big games, he is flashing explosive upside that you don't find lying around in fantasy. After catching one 30-yard pass in the season opener and then missing four games on injured reserve, Cooper has had 100+ yards and a touchdown in consecutive weeks. He caught a 48-yarder in Week 6 against the Patriots and then a 52-yarder and a 60-yarder in Week 7.

Importantly, he's also caught 11 total passes on 12 targets these past two games ... while Garrett Wilson has just six catches on nine targets. I wouldn't say Wilson has been replaced as the WR1, but it is notable that when he draws a defense's toughest matchups or a double-team, Cooper is freed up to thrive against lesser coverage. We'll want to see the shifting target share hold for another couple weeks before drawing any aggressive conclusions, but Cooper is absolutely worth adding on waivers — if he's still available — or you can try to acquire him before the price gets too high.
STOCK DOWN
Garrett Wilson, WR, Jets

We'll start the Stock Down section where we ended the Stock Up. But it's not just Cooper's rise that's hurting Wilson's fantasy value. He had three catches on four targets for 27 yards back in Week 4 against the Bears (with Cooper on IR) and has now logged fewer than seven fantasy points in three of his last four games. And, frankly, this is kind of what Wilson does. He's typically a target monster in New York, but he also tends to underperform, for one reason or another, in far more games than we'd like from a WR1. He's now just the WR24 in points per game on the year and the WR42 over the last month.

As I said with Cooper above, I don't think the roles have reversed in New York, and I expect Wilson to continue putting up strong performances on a near-weekly basis. However, with Cooper breaking out, Wilson's greatest strength — an elite target share — could suffer a hit down the stretch. He's definitely more of a low-end WR2 in my book and I wouldn't mind shopping him for a more consistent producer with a lesser name (or for Zay Flowers).
Chase Brown, RB, Bengals

It's starting to get really ugly for Chase Brown in Cincinnati and in fantasy. He has not topped 39 rushing yards in any of the last three games and has single-digit fantasy totals in four of his last five. The only reason it's not five straight is that he caught 11 passes for 71 yards in an absurd Week 4, but that should not be expected or projected (he's averaged 3.4 catches for 14.4 yards in his other five games). He outproduced Samaje Perine on Sunday, but Perine still managed to vulture a goal-line rushing touchdown. And Joe Burrow carried the offense otherwise, with 292 passing yards and four touchdowns through the air.

Brown is just the RB25 on the season in points per game ... and his best performance was way back in Week 1, when he scored his only touchdown of the year (and just 16.3 points). Since Week 2, he's been outscored by Brian Robinson Jr., Alvin Kamara and Emanuel Wilson, among many others. That's simply not going to cut it for a back drafted to be a fringe RB1. Unless Brown pulls off a major turnaround — as he did down the stretch just last season — he is trending quickly towards bust territory.
Aaron Jones Sr., RB, Vikings

Well, it was a nice run for Aaron Jones Sr. as the solo back in Minnesota. With Jordan Mason on injured reserve from Weeks 2-5 (and a Week 6 bye), Jones averaged a monster 24.3 touches for 110.5 yards per game and was the RB13 in fantasy points per game. In Mason's return on Sunday ... Jones touched the ball nine times and totaled 26 yards. Mason, on the other hand, racked up 15 totes for 68 yards, while playing 62.5% of the snaps (to just 26.8% for Jones).

The only glimmer of hope here might be that the Vikings are about to enter a much tougher stretch of opponents and are very unlikely to continue their unbeaten streak, or at least to do so without struggle. That could mean that game scripts favor Jones (the more active receiver) over Mason for the foreseeable future ... but even if they do, Jones will be an inconsistent half of a committee backfield. It's probably too late to trade him for a decent return, but you simply cannot expect Jones to maintain RB2 fantasy value moving forward.
Isaiah Likely, TE, Giants

The optimistic outlook for Isaiah Likely's Week 7 dud is that the Texans defense found a way to stifle him — which they had done to tight ends all season — and that his disappearance had nothing to do with the J.J. McCarthy takeover at quarterback. Considering Likely caught two of three targets for 44 yards and a touchdown in McCarthy's one quarter two weeks ago, it's not blind optimism ... but there's still reason for concern.

Likely caught just two passes on four targets (for 12 yards) on Sunday, after seeing 11+ targets in each of the three games prior and 9.8 targets per game over the first six weeks. He had been making a case as a top-five tight end, only clearly behind Trey McBride and Brock Bowers, but that case gets a little tougher after 2.2 fantasy points. Heading into a Week 8 bye, Likely, McCarthy and the entire offense will have some time to gel a little further, and I expect things to bounce back a bit on the other side. But it's also possible we just get intermittent disappearances from Likely — he also scored just 2.3 points in Week 3 — as he is not quite the dominant force that McBride or Bowers are.

articles.headline: Roku apps keep crashing before you hit Play? Here's why
keyFacts: Roku apps and operating systems can crash due to bugs, storage limits, or outdated software.
Users can attempt to fix crashes by updating software, restarting the device, or deleting unused apps.
If standard troubleshooting fails, users may need to perform a factory reset or purchase new hardware.
body: Roku apps keep crashing before you hit Play? Here's why
There are a few things you can try to fix it.

Say what you will about Roku in light of its impending takeover by Fox, but its products are a model of simplicity. There's nothing cryptic about its hardware or software controls, and for the most part, Roku has resisted the temptation to jam its OS full of unnecessary visual flair or recommendations. You can be in your favorite streaming app in a matter of seconds.

The platform isn't bulletproof, however. Apps or Roku OS itself can still crash, which might almost be more irritating on a smart TV or media streamer than it is on a computer. Conflicts make sense on complex machines but a Roku device exists almost exclusively to stream video, perhaps with a little music thrown in for good measure. It might not feel far from your microwave refusing to make popcorn.

There are several potential reasons for Roku app crashes, most of which can be solved with one of three actions. There are scenarios, however, where more radical tactics might be needed, including even hardware upgrades. We'll try to steer you away from those.
Why your Roku apps might be crashing, and how to fix it

One possibility is that an app or the OS is buggy in some form. Although all parties try to squash as many bugs as possible, testing is never perfect, especially with so many potential hardware and software combinations out there. Normally, Roku devices update automatically whenever you do a cold boot, or leave your device on for at least 24 to 36 hours. If you want to speed things up, use your remote to navigate to Settings > System > Software update > Check Now. Keep in mind that it can take days or weeks for a patch to be developed.

If updates don't accomplish anything, try restarting your Roku via Settings > System > Power > System restart (the Power menu might be skipped on your device). This gives background processes and the system cache a fresh start, which might be all you need to deal with less severe glitches. In fact, you should be doing this periodically anyway to keep your device running as smoothly as possible.

It might also be time for general housekeeping, by which we mean deleting unused apps. Although Roku apps aren't exactly huge, even the 2024 Roku Ultra only has 4GB of storage, and older or cheaper devices may have less. You could be bumping into the swap space the OS needs, and there's no sense risking that for an app you may never open again.
When extreme measures are called for

If you've tried all of the previous steps and nothing has worked so far, your last-ditch option may be performing a factory reset. This wipes the slate completely clean, reverting your device to the state it was in out of the box — hence the name. This should be avoided whenever possible, since you'll not only have to redownload apps, but reconfigure settings and log back into your accounts. If you're sure you want to try this, head to System > Advanced system settings > Factory reset. Roku also offers hardware-based reset commands if the OS has become totally unusable.

If your device is many years old, an unfortunate possibility is that it may no longer be able to keep up with the latest software. While the company maintains surprisingly extensive update support, newer features and graphics can push the limits of RAM and processor power. You may be bumping up against these barriers, and have no choice but to buy new streaming gear.

There's only so much you can do to hold onto older software releases, unfortunately. Even when Roku has your back, streaming services may decide to cut off older app versions for the sake of security or other plans. You might as well keep updating apps as long as possible.

articles.headline: Meta Muse Makes Marketplace Better. How I Set It Up to Help Me Shop Online
keyFacts: A CNET writer used Meta's AI agent Muse to search Facebook Marketplace for household items like an ottoman, air purifier, and humidifier.
The author said Muse successfully filtered listings by price and location, surfaced relevant items, drafted messages to sellers, and monitored the platform continuously.
The author reported that using Muse saved time compared to manual scrolling and successfully helped arrange a purchase pickup.
body: I have a to-buy list that I never seem to tackle. It’s got the kinds of “adult” items that aren’t necessarily fun to shop for, unlike clothes. Things like furniture, appliances and office equipment. But there are three items I need right now: an ottoman, an air purifier and a humidifier.

Our old ottoman broke, but I’m happy about it. It was dragged along from two previous apartments, and I’ve been wanting to replace it. The air purifier is also necessary, given we’re on the fifth floor and dust tends to cling to everything. With the radiators burning old dust, we’re constantly sneezing. I also promised myself I’d buy a humidifier last winter, so that’s also on the list.

In an effort to snag all three items second-hand, and given that Facebook Marketplace is basically a sport in my area, I put Meta Muse up to the task. I’ve used Muse for shopping and tech support before, but ran into roadblocks with payment and account verification. I had higher hopes using Muse for Marketplace, given it’s a Meta product.
More from CNET
Getting Muse set up
I’d previously used Muse from the chat interface, but this time I went to Ideas in the sidebar and clicked on the specific Marketplace prompt. It’s a recurring task rather than a one-off search.

First, I gave it some parameters around what I was looking for, how far I could travel and what I wanted to pay: “I’m looking for three items: an ottoman, an air purifier and a humidifier. Ideally, in Montclair, NJ, but happy to travel to Manhattan for the air purifier or humidifier if needed. Price-wise, I’d like to pay around $150 for the ottoman, $50 for an air purifier and $50 for a humidifier.”
It immediately surfaced a few options, all within the price range, then noted that it would sweep Facebook Marketplace every 4 hours for new options, which is genuinely helpful.

It even found the air purifier brand I had in mind, and surfaced one that was listed the day before by a five-star seller. For the humidifier, Muse found one in a town that’s hard to get to, so I gave it clearer geographical preferences.

The chat function was helpful, as I was able to ask Muse which brands and models were most expensive and what they retail for, with links to cross-check. What was also cool was Muse’s seller notes. It found a good humidifier in Manhattan, but warned that the seller is new.
I replied by instructing the agent to keep scanning locally as I wasn’t in a rush to buy the humidifier.

I told Muse I was ready to buy the air purifier, and it drafted a message to send to the seller. I made a few edit requests, connected my Messenger to the AI agent, and then Muse took over. I opened Messenger and saw that it had sent the message. Muse checks in every 30 minutes to see if the seller has replied, then notifies me.
While I was waiting, I gave Muse more context around the ottoman. I was after a midcentury style, about the height of a standard lounge and large enough for two people to rest their feet on.

Muse surfaced plenty of options, but this search was less straightforward as it concerned a style choice, too. I pulled one example from the search that I liked and asked Muse for more options like it.

I quickly got through all of the inventory within a 5-mile radius, so I asked Muse to keep monitoring. It would notify me, or I could check in on the Goals tab or click on the Muse avatar and “Upcoming,” which lists every scheduled task.

I assigned Muse to do one more search – to see if my town had any affordable espresso machines or plastic-free coffee brewers. I have my eye on a model, but it’s $400, so I wanted to see what Muse could find.
I loved being able to follow up every find with “Tell me more about this product.” I instructed Muse to send another seller message with the coffee machine it found.
I was on a roll at this point. One last search: an air fryer, but non-toxic. Within minutes, I found one I liked, and Muse messaged them, too.
The verdict on Muse in Marketplace
I was pleasantly surprised by Muse’s Marketplace sweep. It was a much more dynamic experience, being able to narrow the search via the chat function, versus an endless scroll in Marketplace.

Muse scans active searches every 4 hours, which means I’m not missing listings. If a product sells or the seller doesn’t respond, it automatically searches for alternatives. To have this running in the background is super helpful.

It checks before replying to a seller, but I’d rather those messages be in my own voice anyway, and avoid sharing sensitive information with Muse (like my phone number or address). Muse did inform me of some price drops, but it wasn’t for the products I liked.

I saw a seller reply before Muse told me they did (as the agent scans every 30 minutes), so I took over the conversation manually from there. I was able to arrange a pickup — and my list of boring things to buy at last had one checkmark thanks largely to using Muse on Marketplace.

body: Donald Trump intensified his anti-Muslim rhetoric against Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday, portraying him as a threat to national security.

The president also questioned his loyalty to the United States in remarks that drew a sharp rebuke from a former top Arab American ally. Trump called El-Sayed, a former Detroit health official, a “jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists” and would “have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.”

He also repeatedly invoked 9/11, drawing a comparison between stopping El-Sayed from entering the Senate chamber and the passengers who fought back against the hijackers aboard United Flight 93, AP reported.
El-Sayed, who would become the nation’s first Muslim senator if elected, has called attacks on his loyalty to the country “shameful” and repeatedly denied any ties to extremist groups.

The Republican president’s remarks were condemned by Bishara Bahbah, a founder of Arab Americans for Trump, the group that helped lead the president’s outreach to Arab American voters in 2024. “The president’s statements are out of line,” he said in a phone interview. “They are crossing a red line. They are racist.”

Trump also reiterated his apparent love for buxom bums and encouraged the crowd to compliment rapper Nicki Minaj’s behind. The comments about Minaj’s derriere came as he explained his recent observation on the Republican Ohio senator Jon Husted’s rear end.

Earlier in October, Trump said of the former college football player: “I don’t do this with men very often. I started examining his body, because I didn’t know he was a great athlete. And I looked and I watched up and down. I looked at his ass and I looked at the whole – and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands. He’s got these, like, claws.”
“You are a great athlete,” Trump also said to Husted. “Congratulations.” Trump was speaking at the rally to support Mike Rogers, the Michigan Republican Senate candidate.
Read our full report here:
In other developments:

Mary Peltola, a Democrat who is running for Alaska’s lone US Senate seat, and her family suffered minor injuries in a car crash while driving to a campaign stop on Saturday, her campaign said. The family was on its way to the Alaska Federation of Natives annual banquet when another vehicle crashed into the one transporting Peltola and her family, her campaign said in a statement on Sunday. Peltola required medical attention after the collision.

Todd Blanche, Donald Trump’s attorney general, lashed out during an interview on Sunday while defending the justice department’s pre-emptive lawsuit to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate results if the GOP incumbent loses, calling a TV host’s question “crazy”. The testy repartee unfolded on CNN’s State of the Union over the DoJ’s unprecedented legal action, which alleges that there could be “voter confusion” due to two candidates named Dan Sullivan on Alaska’s ballot. Trump told reporters, “I’m the one that said do it” when asked about the suit.

The US military has given Elon Musk’s SpaceX access to restricted space tracking data, raising a new round of questions about whether the Trump administration is attempting to hand over traffic control in Earth’s orbit to a controversial donor. The access also raises new national security questions, industry observers say.

Enrollment in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (Snap) has decreased significantly over the past year in the US following restrictions imposed by the Trump administration, which has forced more people to seek help from food banks or go hungry, stakeholders say. The number of people who receive food stamps has dropped from 41.6 million in July 2025, before the One Big Beautiful Act took effect, to 36.5 million in June 2026, a 13% decrease, according to the latest data from the US Department of Agriculture, which administers the program.
Abdul El-Sayed and other Democratic candidates are embracing universal healthcare. Is it a winning message?
Jessica Glenza

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic US Senate candidate, started his day on the campaign trail in Escanaba, Michigan, where nearby Wisconsin dairy country spills into dense forests and the sandy shores of Green Bay.

This is the upper peninsula – the “UP” – a rural slash of land north of Michigan’s mitt. Electorally, it’s crimson. Donald Trump won some districts near Escanaba by more than 41%. But at the county fairgrounds, past sheds labeled “Beef” and “Swine”, hundreds of locals on the political left have gathered in the hangar-size 4H Club meeting hall to hear El-Sayed speak.
“We built this campaign on three simple things. Y’all remember what they are?” El-Sayed stokes the audience, leading them to a call-and-response.
“Money out of …”
“Politics!”
“Money in your …”
“Pocket!”
“Medicare for …”
“All!”

As Americans prepare for historic cuts enacted in the Republican-led “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”, which is expected to push 17 million people from their health insurance plans, El-Sayed appears to have caught a rising tide of interest in Medicare for All.

This election season, Troy Jackson, the Democratic US Senate candidate from Maine, who’s in a dead heat with Republican Susan Collins, said Medicare for All would be “great coverage”. Angie Nixon, Florida’s Democratic US Senate candidate, has made it a part of her “working families guarantee”. Chris Van Hollen, current US senator for Maryland, added Medicare for All to his platform last December after “listening to his constituents”.

El-Sayed’s supporting act in this series of stops is influential Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a longtime Medicare for All proponent and the subject of whispers about a 2028 presidential run. And, according to an October poll by the health policy thinktank the Kaiser Family Foundation, two-thirds of Americans support the idea.

Technically, Medicare for All is an insurance reform. Proposals currently before Congress would make the federal government into the nation’s health insurer, a “single-payer” system more closely aligned with health systems in peer developed democracies, such as Canada.

Sounds simple. However, in the US, one in every five dollars goes to healthcare. The existing health insurance patchwork fuels profits of world-leading, resource-unlimited corporations and powerful local monopolies. Democrats also worry that replacing private insurance, as Medicare for All advocates call for, would provide fodder for Republicans, who have made stoking popular resentment against government into an electoral strategy.

Those enormous barriers have repeatedly relegated Medicare for All to the political hinterlands. Centrist Democrats worry that, in a nation where me-but-not-thee politics has reigned for many years, Medicare for All is nothing more than a decades-old tried-and-failed idea.

Then again, in a nation where healthcare prices are the highest in the world and climbing, when even the insured find themselves in medical debt, and where the broad-daylight assassination of an insurance executive elicits catharsis and not mourning – the yearning for change is personal and visceral.
“Not enough doctors, not enough healthcare,” says El-Sayed, who ran both the Detroit and Wayne county health departments, and received a medical degree from Columbia University.

El-Sayed’s campaign comes as the Trump administration enacts the largest federal healthcare cut in the nation’s history – extracting $1tn from the system primarily by through severe cuts to Medicaid, the federal-state health insurance program for low-income and disabled people. Medicaid cuts are expected to close hospitals, particularly those in rural outposts like Escanaba, and the urban core.

At the same time, some of the most popular health policies of recent years – such as reining in medical debt collections – spring directly from the policy work of Medicare for All advocates. Add to this a counterintuitive reality: almost half of all healthcare today is already paid for by federal, state or local government, according to the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

WSJ reports that Trump administration is eyeing ousted Hungarian strongman to lead United Nations

A Wall Street Journal op-ed published on Sunday has raised the possibility that the Trump administration will push Viktor Orbán, the longtime illiberal leader of Hungary, to help the United Nations as its new secretary general.

The report, citing sources from three different countries, said that the Trump administration believed China and Russia would back Orbán as a candidate (Orbán was perhaps Russian president Vladimir Putin’s closest ally in the European Union).

Orbán has been free for the job since losing his re-election bid earlier this year. Before then, he was a close ally of President Trump and, thanks to his hardline policies on immigration and LGBTQ+ rights, as well as his crackdowns on academics, independent media and NGOs, an ideological figurehead of rightwing populists around the world. JD Vance even traveled to Hungary to stump for his re-election.

Candidates for the UN secretary general are voted on by the entire UN general assembly. But to get before that body, they must first win the blessing of the 15-member security council, and its five permanent members: the US, Russia, China, France and the United Kingdom. Those five can veto any candidate they dislike. If Russia and China were to buy into Orbán’s candidacy, it would leave only France and the UK with the veto power to block him.
Discontent with Trump buoys Democrats in Ohio: ‘People are disgusted by the corruption’
Stephen Starr
Democrat Kim McCarthy is canvassing in a middle-class Ohio neighborhood of four-bedroom, three-bathroom homes. There are $70,000 trucks in the driveways and robot lawnmowers at work.
“This is a neighborhood of two incomes and young families; people working hard,” says McCarthy, who is running against a three-time Republican incumbent for a seat in Ohio’s house of representatives.

Despite the manicured lawns, these are the very Ohioans struggling from the fallout of many of the Trump administration’s policies. They live in a district that includes the largest single-site employer in Ohio – the Wright-Patterson air force base – whose civilian contractors and employees have been hit hard by federal workforce cuts. Rising mortgage interest rates and wider affordability concerns are top of mind for many.

McCarthy’s opponent, Brian Lampton, beat her in a previous election by 15 points. In the presidential election two years ago, Trump won 60% of the vote here in Fairborn. But having knocked on thousands of Greene county doors, she says she’s noticed something different this year: people are telling her on the doorstep that they are planning to vote Democrat down the ballot for the first time.
“One woman I was speaking to earlier who worked in the military and recently retired was like: ‘Oh my God, I can’t afford anything.’ You could kind of see the sadness in her eyes,” she says.

For more than a decade, Ohio has been considered a firm Republican stronghold, but after 20 months of extreme Trump administration policies, signs of discontent with the status quo are appearing here. That could be critical for Democrats at every level on the ballot – the party is trying to reclaim a US Senate seat, the governor’s mansion, and a host of competitive house seats around the state.
Early voting indicators in Ohio suggest that participation among affiliated Democrats is higher this year when compared to 2024, especially in predominantly Republican districts.

According to the Ohio secretary of state’s data portal website, by 13 October more early voting ballots were returned in rural Defiance county by Democratic affiliated voters than by Republicans, despite Trump winning 69% of the vote in the county in the 2024 presidential election.
The county also had the highest ballot return rate in the state, at 19%, suggesting a high level of motivation.

The economy isn’t the only thing on voters’ minds. “The number one issue in Defiance right now is the proposed datacenter. There is a local investor who is entertaining the idea of selling property to a datacenter investor,” says Rebecca Kirkland of the Defiance County Democratic party.

Trump has repeatedly encouraged communities to accept datacenters, telling supporters at a campaign rally outside Dayton, on 3 October, “We want them,” despite broad bipartisan opposition to their presence.

Home to a General Motors powertrain foundry that employs more than 500 people, Defiance county has also been hit hard by Trump’s tariffs war on Canada: among the plant’s main customers is the GM-owned St Catharines engine plant in Ontario, with engine parts that are built in Defiance are shipped for assembly across the Canadian border.
“There aren’t many high-paying jobs available in this area. We see posts on community Facebook pages of people looking for assistance finding work, housing or financial assistance,” says Kirkland.

Still, in a state that for decades turned older and whiter and was won by Trump in the last three presidential elections, Democrats know the odds are stacked against them. And pollsters are cautioning that the surge in early voting might not indicate that more Ohioans will vote for Democrats by the end of the election.
US military ready to launch new, large-scale attacks on Iran, media report says

American military forces are in place and waiting on a command from President Trump to launch a major new military operation against Iran, CNN has reported, citing a pair of US officials with knowledge of the plans.

The scale of those attacks, the outlet reported, would probably go beyond the strikes the US has traded with Iran in recent months. Other officials who spoke with CNN said that it seemed like Trump was leaning toward moving ahead with such an operation, probably before the end of the year and possibly after the midterm elections.

The war in Iran, which Trump launched alongside Israel at the end of February, has made that election an uphill battle for the Republicans. The conflict, unpopular at its outset, has sent energy prices soaring after Iran retaliated by closing the strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping artery for oil and gas. But Trump has doubled down on the conflict while on the campaign trail, alleging that Iran wants Democrats to win control of Congress, and that only he can keep the country from obtaining nuclear weapons.

The report also comes as intelligence has surfaced suggesting Iran and its allies are in advanced stages of planning attacks against Americans in the Middle East, spurring the Trump administration to take measures to protect US personnel.

Donald Trump will still be US president on the morning of 4 November. But he could be facing a very different political landscape, depending on the results of the US midterm elections held the previous day.

As the name implies, midterm elections fall nearly halfway through a president’s term. They are often a telling referendum on the sitting president’s performance, something Trump is actively encouraging by telling voters “pretend I’m on the ballot”. In this case, voters will decide whether Trump’s Republican party can retain its grip on Congress.

Democrats are hoping to capitalise on growing discontent with Trump to seize control of the US House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate. Republicans are fighting to preserve their congressional majorities and prevent a fresh period of legislative paralysis and investigations into the White House.

Lula's victory in Brazil hinders Trump's ambitions in Latin America

Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s overnight re-election victory – a stunning reversal after he trailed in the previous round of voting against right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro – represents a blow to President Trump’s political ambitions in Latin America.

Lula, who secured a fourth non-consecutive term in office, had campaigned on protecting Brazil’s sovereignty in the face of alleged US coercion and colonialism, and had accused the US of seeking to meddle in the country’s elections.

And while Trump did not outright support the defeated candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, he is the son of one of Trump’s former close allies in the region, ousted Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro. The older Bolsonaro is currently serving a prison sentence for attempting to overturn the results of his 2022 election defeat to Lula. Those criminal proceedings prompted Trump to at one point slap steep tariffs on Brazil, deepening the divide between Trump and the Brazilian leader.
Trump has yet to publicly weigh in on Lula’s victory. But Trump’s son, Donald Trump Jr, took to social media to criticize a decision to extend voting in Brazil for two hours.

Anthropic’s Claude AI model accessed Georgia voter data in US
Dan Milmo
Anthropic’s Claude model accessed voter data in the US state of Georgia, the AI company has confirmed, in the latest example of unauthorised behaviour by the technology.

The AI model managed to bypass a paywall to reach data that is publicly available but is typically accessible only after paying a fee. Claude accessed aggregate vote counts as part of a statistics project at Anthropic, which is preparing for a $1.5tn (£1.1tn) flotation.

“Claude did not access the state’s voter registration system, change any voting records, or pull any individual voter records,” Anthropic said, adding that it has since taken steps to block similar actions.

Anthropic said the AI found a loophole in an old version of the state agency’s website, discovering that it issues a digital entry pass – an “access token” – to visitors, which resulted in it requesting a token and gaining access to the information.
The AI developer said it had since put in place guardrails to prevent similar actions happening again. The incident was first reported by the news website Axios.

US voters are exhausted by years of higher prices. Donald Trump won the presidency in 2024 on promises to lower inflation and undo the damage he said the Biden administration had inflicted on the economy.

In Trump’s view, his plan is working. At a recent rally in Montana, Trump boasted about the current economy, framing it as a booming time for Americans. “We’re richer now,” he said. “We don’t have inflation.”

Economic data paints a different picture. Inflation, especially gas prices, have soared over the last year. The job market has been in stasis, and higher interest rates have meant it’s more expensive for Americans to borrow money for loans and mortgages.

These fluctuations have a concrete impact on the lives of Americans. A recent Harris poll for the Guardian found that a majority of Americans, including some Republicans, disagree.
