articles.headline: A galaxy united: ‘Save Mass Effect’ movement gains traction with petition, Shepard voice actors’ support, and more
keyFacts: Fans and developers launched a Save Mass Effect movement after EA canceled the upcoming game and shut down BioWare last week.
A Change.org petition gathered over 214,000 signatures with support from Commander Shepard voice actors Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer.
A fan rented a billboard in Times Square and developers of a related upcoming title posted on Twitter to support the petition.
body: It’s always nice to see people come together in support of something they love.

Like Commander Shepard rallying the galaxy to fight the Reapers in Mass Effect 3, the Mass Effect community is now banding together to try and save the franchise after its upcoming game was canceled as part of EA shutting down BioWare last week.

Image via BioWare Since the news came down that the work-in-progress title was canned, along with the layoffs of the remainder of the people working at BioWare, the community has been in an uproar. A dev who worked on the upcoming Mass Effect: Universe leaked concept footage of the game in action , and a YouTuber who was part of a “council” to give feedback revealed a slew of exciting details .

And in the process, the greater gaming community rallied to take action. A Change.org petition named #SaveMassEffect has now reached over 214,000 signatures and climbing, helped in part by support from Commander Shepard actors Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer.

“Join us in this mission to secure the future of the Mass Effect universe by signing and sharing this petition,” the petition states. “Let’s prominently illustrate to EA the significance of this iconic series and our collective demand for its continued journey across the stars. Sign today and keep the spirit of exploration alive!”

But it didn’t stop there. Mass Effect fan @KalaElizabeth has rented out a billboard in New York’s Times Square to spread the word. Even the devs behind The Expanse: Osiris Reborn , a 2027 title heavily inspired by Mass Effect , posted on Twitter/X in support of the petition in hopes that it will spur a change somewhere, anywhere, to keep the franchise alive somehow.
I like it too.
Hold the line. #MassEffect #SaveMassEffect #N7 #MassEffectIsAlive #CommanderShepard https://t.co/uQJ4x5mXPS pic.twitter.com/vx22yejYbR
— Mark Meer (@Mark_Meer) October 24, 2026
Just bought our first billboard for #SaveMassEffect ! pic.twitter.com/U26E6YAAxM
— Kala Elizabeth #SaveMassEffect (@kalaelizabeth) October 25, 2026

It’s clear that the franchise’s fans are not willing to go down without a fight despite EA’s decision to shutter it all. Will this outcry cause anything to change? Who knows, but this has been a year of gamers using their voices to speak out against all sorts of things, like PlayStation’s decision to end disc-based games in 2028, or Destiny 2’s end-of-service.
As a Mass Effect fan myself, I hope that EA feels the pressure to sell the IP to someone who will do it justice rather than let it rot.

The company reported losses of over $80 billion in the first half of the year alongside $16.3 billion in revenue.
Anthropic stated it will pursue investments that may seem irresponsibly large to capture technological opportunities.
body: - Anthropic has revealed further details on plans to list on the stock market
- The company will be the first AI firm to go public and is likely to debut with a valuation exceeding SpaceX's record
- The company plans to make investments 'that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance'

AI giant Anthropic has revealed more details on its plans to go public in what is likely to be the biggest stock market debut in history - higher than SpaceX’s record breaking valuation of $1.8 trillion earlier this year.

The company, which announced its plans to go public back in June 2026, will also be the AI firm to go public. OpenAI has also announced plans to become a publicly traded company shortly after, but will likely debut on the market early next year.

Anthropic has reported losses of more than $80.7 billion in the first half of the year, with a revenue of $16.3 billion over the same period. The company will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ‘ANT’.
‘Irresponsibly large’ investments still to come
Despite these financials, the company has said it will make investments “that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance.”

“In order to fully capture the opportunity in front of us, we need to invest more aggressively than would a business that operates in a more slowly changing technological regime," Anthropic said. "In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets."

As part of being listed as a publicly traded company, Anthropic will have to provide greater visibility into the company’s finances - including whether or not the company is currently profitable. Much of the economic growth in the US is currently driven by AI companies, and the greater transparency into the finances of one of the biggest AI companies in the world could have serious implications for the economy.
The company has not revealed how many shares will be released, nor their price range.

articles.headline: Crucial swing voters troubled by DSA, new poll shows: ‘Souring on socialism’
keyFacts: A new Americans for Prosperity report shows 56% of surveyed swing voters hold an unfavorable view of the Democratic Socialists of America.
The report indicates nearly 60% of respondents believe the Democratic Party is controlled by the far left.
The survey also revealed 45% of respondents trust Democrats more on cost of living issues, compared to 36% for Republicans.
body: WASHINGTON — Crucial US swing voters have become increasingly troubled by the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America and the far-left in general — a major warning sign for Dems ahead of the midterms, a new poll shows.

When asked about their views of the DSA, 56% of respondents indicated they had an unfavorable view, up from 50% in September, according to Americans for Prosperity’s latest “Americans Unscripted” report.
Nearly 60% also felt the Democratic Party was controlled by the far left, again up from 50% in September, and 82% indicated they favor personal freedom and free markets over government control.
“Swing voters are souring on socialism — and fast,” AFP spokeswoman Katelyn Bledsoe told The Post.
“That’s a real opening for Republicans, and the candidates who show voters a credible plan to bring their costs down are in the strongest position on November 3.”

Americans for Prosperity, a libertarian-leaning policy advocacy group associated with the billionaire Koch brothers, has been leaning on its network of organizers across the country to get a pulse check. This is its last “Americans Unscripted” report before the Nov. 3 elections.
The question about the DSA was asked to about 9,000 to 10,200 people in eight states: Alaska, Iowa, Michigan, Montana, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio and Wisconsin.
Critically, the trend from September to October indicates that swing voters who will be deciding key races are increasingly turning on the far left.
“Nothing is free,” a man named Michael from Holland, Mich., told an Americans for Prosperity volunteer, according to the report. “There’s an agenda behind all these promises of free benefits.”
Still, there are some red flags for Republicans in the survey as well.
Strikingly, 45% of respondents sampled indicated they trusted Democrats more on cost of living issues, compared to 36% who said Republicans and 18% who said neither.
That marks a turnaround from August, when Republicans had a 44% to 39% edge over Democrats.

articles.headline: Major school district's pledge with teachers' union sparks racial discrimination complaint
keyFacts: Defending Education filed a federal civil rights complaint against Cherry Creek School District alleging employment discrimination based on race.
The complaint targets a 2023 agreement between the district and its teachers union to recruit, retain, and advance educators of color.
Defending Education asked the U.S. Department of Education Office for Civil Rights to open an investigation into the district.
body: FIRST ON FOX: One of Colorado's largest school districts is facing a new federal civil rights complaint over a pledge it made with its teachers' union to recruit, retain and advance educators of color.

Defending Education filed a federal civil rights complaint Monday, which was first obtained by Fox News Digital, with the U.S. Department of Education alleging that CCSD is discriminating on the basis of race in employment. CCSD is notably Colorado’s fourth-largest school district, and serves 52,000 students and more than 300,000 residents in the southeast Denver metropolitan area, according to the district’s website.

At the heart of the complaint is the district's June 2023 " Educators of Color Declaration," which commits Cherry Creek School District and its teacher’s union to recruiting, retaining and advancing educators of color, even as a separate provision in the same agreement calls for recruitment, hiring and advancement to be based on qualifications without regard to race.

"Cherry Creek Schools has written racial preferences directly into its teachers’ contract. The district’s ‘Educators of Color Declaration’ commits it to recruiting, retaining, and promoting teachers based on the color of their skin — which means other equally qualified teachers are passed over for the same reason," Sarah Parshall Perry, Vice President and Senior Legal Fellow at Defending Education, told Fox News Digital.

"That's not diversity; it's discrimination, and it is precisely what Title VI and the Fourteenth Amendment forbid. The Supreme Court could not have been clearer in Students for Fair Admissions: the law is colorblind, and a school district cannot cure a race-based hiring policy with generic 'equal opportunity' language."

Title VI prohibits race discrimination in federally funded programs under specified conditions, while Title VII more directly governs employment discrimination, leaving the legality of Cherry Creek's teacher recruitment and advancement commitments dependent on how those policies are implemented.
OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE CLEARS WAY FOR WHITE EMPLOYEE TO CHALLENGE SEATTLE'S DEI POLICIES

The "Educators of Color Declaration" also commits the district and its teachers' union to intentionally recruiting highly qualified educators of color while making a concerted effort to retain those already employed by the district and help them advance into leadership positions, according to the district's negotiated agreement.
JUSTICE DEPARTMENT LAUNCHES TITLE VI INVESTIGATION INTO DEI PROGRAMS AT ARIZONA STATE UNIVERSITY

Additionally, the policy says that "to fulfill these goals, all policies in this agreement shall reflect Cherry Creek School District core values by grounding the work of negotiations in diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI)," according to the school district's 2026-2027 Negotiated Agreement.
FLORIDA STATE UNIVERSITY HIT WITH FEDERAL CIVIL RIGHTS INVESTIGATION OVER RACE, SEX-BASED SCHOLARSHIP PROGRAMS

"Cherry Creek is under no obligation to accept federal funding, but because it has, it cannot run a racial balancing scheme for its own workforce and still adhere to federal law," Perry continued. "We are asking the Office for Civil Rights to open an investigation and put an end to it."

Defending Education's latest complaint comes after the Department of Education announced a separate investigation on June 8, into allegations that Cherry Creek School District sponsored racially discriminatory programs involving students, teachers and parents.

"These allegations of racially discriminatory conduct in this District seem to permeate almost every aspect of the school community, affecting students, teachers, and parents alike," Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights Kimberly Richey said in a statement at the time. "Federal law prohibits racial discrimination, which means that race cannot be a factor in how the school educates its students or trains its teachers."

The Trump administration has been cracking down on DEI efforts across the nation's education system, including proposing new regulations in September that would revoke the tax-exempt status of private schools and colleges that consider race in admissions, scholarships or other school-administered programs.
CCSD did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment on Monday.
When reached for comment, a Department of Education spokesperson told Fox News Digital that "the Department does not confirm complaints."

articles.headline: The Republican Party kept its promises. The rest is up to you
keyFacts: Tea Party Patriots Action Chairman Jenny Beth Martin wrote that President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans delivered on their 2024 campaign promises.
The article stated that Border Patrol encounters fell to their lowest level in over 50 years and Congress made the 2017 tax cuts permanent.
Martin stated that more than 260,000 federal employees left government service in 2025 following workforce reductions by the administration.
body: With early voting already underway in many states, the most compelling case for voting to keep the GOP majorities in the House and Senate is simple. President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans campaigned in 2024 on an ambitious agenda. And they have delivered.

The Republican agenda emphasizes individual liberty, less government, and the rule of law. In each area, the GOP-controlled Congress has achieved visible results that provide a stark contrast with the Biden years.
Consider the headlines that were a routine part of American life during Biden’s one term in office.

Unprecedented numbers of illegal border crossings at our southern border were an everyday news item, as Americans witnessed the breakdown of law and order and a rapid increase in violent crimes as the humanitarian crisis enveloped entire government agencies.

Other headlines in the news showcased the ever-expanding federal government, as the Biden administration expanded the federal workforce by 130,000 employees, handing over new and expansive enforcement operations. The federal government’s size and reach grew to levels Americans had never seen before.
At the same time, the Democrats promised to fund their ever-growing federal government through higher taxes. Those tax hikes were set to go into effect with the expiration of the Trump 2017 Tax Cuts.

Trump and Republicans in Congress crafted a specific agenda to address each of these spiraling problems. They pledged to bring a halt to the inflow of illegal immigrants. They promised that the days of out-of-control and unaccountable government would come to an end. And a signature part of the GOP’s platform was an extension of the tax cuts, preventing the largest tax hike in U.S. history.
So where do things stand today, twenty-one months into Trump’s second term?

The southern border is no longer an entry point for millions of illegal immigrants. In fact, according to a Pew Research Center analysis of federal data, Border Patrol encounters at the U.S.-Mexico border fell to their lowest annual level in more than 50 years during fiscal year 2025. Since February 2025, monthly encounters have remained below 10,000, a dramatic reduction from the levels recorded during the Biden administration. The radical change at our southern border is the unmistakable evidence of the Republicans’ promise kept.

On the tax front, Congress enacted legislation in 2025 making permanent the lower individual income tax rates established by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, preventing their scheduled expiration. The legislation also preserved the expanded standard deduction, made permanent the 20% deduction for qualifying small-business income, and restored immediate expensing for certain business investments and domestic research and development costs. These provisions provided certainty for families and for job-creators as they planned their budgets. Preserving those tax cuts also meant that Americans could keep more of their hard-earned money.

Republicans further acted on their promise to reduce the size of the federal bureaucracy. On his first day in office, Trump established the Department of Government Efficiency, commonly referred to as DOGE, to identify wasteful spending, reduce federal employment, and reorganize government operations. DOGE pursued agency restructuring, contract cancellations, and workforce reductions. More than 260,000 federal employees left government service during 2025 under the administration’s broader workforce policies.

The Republicans ’ commitment to reducing the federal government’s workforce is directly linked to two aspects of conservatives’ agenda. First is the well-established fact that nothing is free in life, and nothing is more expensive than a government program. Americans necessarily foot the bill when government grows. The second aspect is that a bigger federal government is a busier federal government, crafting onerous new regulations and interfering with economic growth.

The past 21 months demonstrate a clear contrast between the Democrats’ failures and the Republicans’ accomplishments. Americans have benefited from the Republicans’ rule-of-law approach to immigration policy, lower taxes, and a scaled-back federal government.

The Democrats on the ballot this cycle aren’t shying away from their promises to reverse everything the Republicans have accomplished. They are actually promising to undo the Trump tax cuts, revert back to the unrestricted immigration, and swell the federal government again.
THE EXECUTIVE BRANCH NEEDS AN EXECUTIVE

That’s the state of play for Americans as they cast their ballots this midterm election. There’s the hope that Republicans will win and continue delivering on their popular promises. And there’s the fear that Democrats will win and begin reversing those policies, bringing back higher taxes, weaker border enforcement, and a more intrusive federal government.
America is stronger today because Republicans kept their promises and have devoted themselves to implementing an agenda that prioritizes Americans.

articles.headline: Last call for The Register ’s data sovereignty dinner in Washington
keyFacts: The Register is hosting a dinner in Washington on October 29 featuring representatives from HPE and NVIDIA to discuss sovereign AI infrastructure.
Editor-in-chief Matt Rosoff will chair the event, which features no slides or recordings and operates under the Chatham House Rule.
The invitation-only event is intended for technology, data, and risk leaders from regulated industries including healthcare, finance, and government.
body: This Thursday, 29 October, The Register hosts HPE and NVIDIA at one dinner table in Washington to answer the question that stalls AI in regulated industries: where the data lives, who can reach it, and what an auditor will accept as evidence a year from now. The table is nearly set. If you have been meaning to ask for a place, this is the week.

Editor-in-chief Matt Rosoff chairs. HPE sends Bharath Ramesh, Head of Product, AI Factory Solutions, and Tracy Mills, Acting Director Federal Systems Integrators and Distinguished Chief Technologist Federal. NVIDIA sends Bert Condensa, Vice President for Enterprise AI Factory Segment Sales. They are there to take questions, with no slides and no recording, and the chair stops a pitch before it starts.

The evening runs under the Chatham House Rule. That is the point of it. The things worth knowing about sovereign AI infrastructure, such as what a bank had to rebuild or which option somebody paid for and would not buy again, get said at a table like this and nowhere else.
The agenda: which infrastructure options hold a boundary, what each one costs, and whether any of it survives production.

The seats are for technology, data and risk leaders in healthcare, financial services, research, pharmaceuticals, government and higher education. Dinner runs from 6.00pm to 8.30pm at Fiola Mare, Washington DC. Places go by invitation and the last of them are going now.
Request one here .
Government and public sector guests: where your agency’s ethics rules require it, you can pay your own share and we will provide a receipt. Please say so when you request an invitation.

articles.headline: Heroes Never Die, a Survivor-Plus-Tactics Strategy Game, Announced for PC
keyFacts: Developer Ludogram announced Heroes Never Die, a fantasy strategy game combining survival mechanics and tactical decisions, for PC release in 2027.
Players can choose from over 20 heroes across four factions, battling monster hordes and rival heroes while upgrading towns and building armies.
Creative director Edouard Gaudel stated that the team is delighted to announce the project and invited players to join an upcoming private playtest.
body: If you've ever wondered what a fusion of Vampire Survivors and Heroes of Might and Magic would look like, then Heroes Never Die might be the game for you. It's a newly announced fantasy strategy game from developer Ludogram that "aims to take the best of the survival formula and fuse it with more tactical decisions, real-time army building, and powerful fantasy heroes." It will be released in 2027 for PC.

In Heroes Never Die, you'll choose your titular hero – there are over 20 in the lineup – and battle not just monster hordes but also rival heroes. Each hero has their own skills, but no matter who you pick, you'll seek to upgrade your town by gathering resources and fighting foes. There are also four factions and over 60 different units, with the developers promising that no two runs will be alike.

“We’re delighted to finally announce Heroes Never Die, a project we’ve been working on in the shadows for a couple of years”, said creative director Edouard Gaudel. “We cannot wait to see our first players fighting hordes of monsters, and evolving their armies while meeting our heroes. Don’t forget to join our upcoming Playtest!”
If you're interested, you can sign up for the private playtest and/or wishlist Heroes Never Die on Steam .

articles.headline: Why Ukraine may be involved in Mali's conflict
keyFacts: An investigation by CNN reported that around 15 Ukrainian drone specialists are supporting Tuareg rebels in northern Mali to weaken Russian influence.
Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso accused Ukraine of supporting armed groups, leading them to sever diplomatic relations and deepen ties with Russia.
Experts warn that any potential Ukrainian cooperation with Tuareg separatists carries political risks because the rebels collaborate with the jihadist group JNIM.
body: Ukraine is fighting Russia — and the conflict may extend into Africa's Sahel region.

According to an investigation published by US media outlet CNN this month, around 15 Ukrainian drone specialists are reportedly supporting Tuareg rebels in northern Mali. Their common enemy: the military government in Bamako and its Russian allies.
But how reliable is the information? And what price could Kyiv pay for engaging in Africa?

Marta Oliynyk-D'omochko, coordinator of the African Studies Program at the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy, sees a strategic motive. "Ukraine's main interest is to weaken Russia's influence around the world," she told DW. If Russia's military influence were rolled back, she added, the economic opportunities arising from it would also diminish.

Russian historian Irina Filatova, professor emeritus at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, also considers Ukrainian support for the Tuareg movement plausible. However, she says she has no independent evidence to confirm such involvement.

Kyiv's alleged partners are controversial. The Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) cooperates with the Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal Muslimeen (JNIM), a jihadist group affiliated with al-Qaeda.
Suspicions dating back to 2024
In July 2024, DW reported on possible involvement by the Ukrainian military intelligence service (HUR) in an ambush on Russian Wagner fighters near Tinzaouaten in northern Mali.
At the time, HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov said the Tuareg rebels had received information they needed to carry out the attack. Ukraine denied direct involvement.
Paramilitaries from Russia's Wagner Group and Malian troops suffered heavy losses in the July 2024 attack.
CNN's investigation has reignited the question of whether the Russia-Ukraine war is also being fought on African soil.
Signals from Kyiv, but no confirmation

The suspicions were renewed by a post on X by Kyrylo Budanov. The former head of Ukraine's military intelligence, now chief of staff to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on September 7 that Ukrainian intelligence protects the country's interests worldwide — "from Russia to Africa … in the burning desert sands and in the snows of icy Antarctica...".

Budanov did not explicitly mention Mali and his post does not confirm any specific operation. CNN reported that the Ukrainians provided drone training, operational planning and remote support for drone missions. DW has not independently verified those claims.

DW reached out to the HUR for comment. Among other things, DW wanted to know whether personnel had been deployed to Mali, whether the political leadership had approved such a mission, and what measures were in place to ensure that the JNIM — which cooperates with the FLA — does not indirectly benefit from Ukrainian support.
DW did not receive a specific response. An HUR spokesperson said the agency might provide information at a later date. The extent of any potential Ukrainian involvement therefore remains unclear.
Why Mali matters to Kyiv

Following military coups in 2020 and 2021, Mali increasingly turned away from Western partners and toward Russia. The Wagner Group was subsequently replaced by the Africa Corps in 2025 as Moscow reorganized its military presence.
Russia has sought to consolidate its influence in the Sahel region and present itself as a reliable security partner.
Ulf Laessing, former head of the Sahel program of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation in Mali and now head of Konrad's Syria and Iraq program, says Russia is continuing to expand its activities in Africa.

"I have received information that the Africa Corps still uses Syria and Libya as transit points for flights from Russia, including for refueling and loading, to support its operations on the continent," Laessing told DW.
From Ukraine's perspective, it could be attractive to exert pressure on Russian forces in Africa.

Filatova sees a strategic logic to this: "The Ukrainians regard Russian troops anywhere in the world as legitimate targets." Setbacks in Mali could tie up Russian resources and undermine Moscow's reputation as a security partner, she argued.

However, Oliynyk-D'omochko stresses that the relationship with the Tuareg is not a comprehensive alliance. The FLA is not seeking to replace the government in Bamako. Instead, it is focused on northern Mali and is pursuing self-determination or extensive autonomy.
Oliynyk-D'omochko describes the relationship as a tactical arrangement: "It is more of a situational alliance against a common enemy than a comprehensive partnership."
The alliance with jihadists

The FLA is fighting for an independent state in the north of Mali, a region predominantly inhabited by Tuaregs. JNIM, by contrast, aims to impose strict Islamic rule. Both groups oppose the military government and its Russian allies, but their objectives differ.

Any potential Ukrainian support for the FLA would not, in itself, prove that Kyiv is directly supporting JNIM. However, jihadists could benefit indirectly if they conduct joint operations with FLA or gain access to knowledge and equipment.
Cooperation between Tuareg and Islamist groups dates back more than a decade.

After the ousting and killing of Libya's longtime dictator Muammar al-Gaddafi during the Arab Spring in October 2011, heavily armed Tuareg fighters returned to Mali and took up the struggle for an independent state.
In the process, separatist ambitions became intertwined with Islamist movements. Iyad Ag Ghaly, the current leader of JNIM, was himself involved in the Tuareg rebellion before turning to jihadism.

According to Oliynyk-D'omochko, the cooperation is primarily tactical in nature. The two sides have collaborated during past uprisings but later fell out. It remains unclear how long the current alliance will last.

For Kyiv, this also poses a political risk. In many African countries, the Tuaregs are viewed as separatists. Cooperation with them could therefore create the impression that Ukraine is interfering in another country's internal affairs.
Claims of support for armed groups

Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso accuse Ukraine of supporting armed groups and threatening their territorial integrity. The three Sahel nations, all ruled by military governments, have severed diplomatic relations with Kyiv and deepened their cooperation with Russia.

In September, Mali's Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop accused Ukraine at the United Nations of "providing clear and open support to terrorist groups and other mafia-like groups to undermine our country's territorial integrity," reported Agence France-Presse. Diop did not provide evidence for his claim.
The three nations' governments have may have an interest in legitimizing their partnership with Moscow and portraying Kyiv as a destabilizing actor.
Filatova considers Ukrainian activities in the region plausible but says she has no evidence to substantiate the accusations.

Oliynyk-D'omochko has likewise found no definitive proof. At the same time, she warns of the potential consequences for Ukraine's Africa policy: Kyiv advocates equal partnerships with African countries. Any alleged cooperation with separatists could undermine that message and affect how potential partners view Ukraine.
What price could Ukraine pay?

Engagement in Mali could offer Ukraine a relatively low-cost way to weaken Russian interests beyond Europe. A small team of specialists could train local fighters and improve their capabilities in the use of drones.

But a potential partnership with the FLA carries political risks. Because the Tuareg separatists cooperate with the JNIM, Kyiv could face accusations of indirectly supporting Islamist fighters. That could undermine Ukraine's efforts to strengthen its relations with African countries.
This article has been translated from German

articles.headline: F1 in Texas: The American race that fans love to attend
keyFacts: Formula 1 returned to the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas, for its annual American race.
Unlike the temporary street circuits in Miami and Las Vegas, COTA is a permanent track featuring various elevation changes and challenging turns.
COTA has added landscaping, hospitality structures with swimming pools, and amusement rides along its fringes as part of a diversification strategy.
body: AUSTIN, Texas—Formula 1 returned to US shores this weekend with its annual visit to the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas. Once in danger of falling off the calendar due to a lack of interest, it’s now one of the most popular tracks on the calendar and, of the US’s three races, it’s the one the real fans mostly attend.

Unlike Miami or Las Vegas, which race on temporary street circuits, COTA is a permanent race track with plenty of run-off areas instead of concrete walls. Designed by motorcycle racer Kevin Schwanz—Herman Tilke’s company did only the buildings and infrastructure, contrary to popular belief—the track combines a mix of corner speeds with challenging turn sequences, a few heavy braking zones, and plenty of elevation changes.

It’s a place Ars knows rather intimately by now. We’ve driven it in everything from an Audi TT-S to a Corvette ZR1 to a bicycle, and that’s just in the real world. Over the years, we’ve been there for F1 to learn about how the sport puts together its broadcasts, how Pirelli designs its tires, and how various tech partners help teams manage their data and strategies. We even saw the race through a neophyte’s eyes. And that’s just F1—we’ve logged many hours there with the World Endurance Championship and IMSA for the Lone Star Le Mans races in sweaty September.

It’s changed a lot since I attended the first USGP back in 2012. There’s more landscaping. The grassy banks that surround the track are now covered in hospitality structures, including one connected to the paddock building by cable car, complete with not one but two swimming pools. Along its fringes, the skyline is now studded with rollercoasters and amusement rides, part of COTA’s diversification strategy that combines theme park, concert venue, and, of course, a place to race.

articles.headline: The horse that ushered in Manchester United’s tragic arc | Jonathan Wilson
keyFacts: Manchester United is facing another managerial crisis following a 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth.
A 2003 legal dispute over the racehorse Rock of Gibraltar led to a falling out between manager Alex Ferguson and major shareholders John Magnier and JP McManus.
The shareholders sold their stake to Malcolm Glazer, enabling a 2005 leveraged buyout that plunged the club into long-term debt.
body: And so here we are again, at that point as the nights draw in and Manchester United prepare to sack a manager. Autumn: season of mists, mellow fruitfulness and a crisis at Old Trafford. Sunday’s 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth, coming on the back of last week’s 4-1 reverse against Como, made clear what many had feared from the moment Michael Carrick was given the job on a permanent basis: that he isn’t up to it.

But then, who could be? When you’ve burned through a long list of managers in 13 years, it’s perhaps worth considering whether the manager is really the problem. Could some blame perhaps go to the director of football, Jason Wilcox, or the chief executive, Omar Berrada, the people making the appointments? Or perhaps to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the cost-cutting tax exile and minority shareholder with responsibility for sporting operations? Or to the Glazer family, who plunged the club into debt with a leveraged buyout in 2005 and have since made calamitous decision after calamitous decision, reducing the most successful club in English league history to a mid-table laughing stock with a roof that leaks symbolically?

It’s worth remembering where all this began. The United story has taken on the aspect of a classical tragedy and, like all good tragedies, it begins with a small, seemingly unconnected moment, amplified by pride, that ends up bringing the whole edifice crashing down.

In 1999, Mull of Kintyre, a horse owned by the Irish millionaire John Magnier, won the Gimcrack Stakes at York. Traditionally, the winning owner would give a speech at the Gimcrack Dinner, but Magnier was a shy man who hated public speaking so he asked his friend, the United manager Alex Ferguson, to give the speech on his behalf. The racing establishment, though, refused: it had to be the owner. To spite them, Magnier named Ferguson as the owner of another horse, Juniper. The following year, Juniper was narrowly beaten in the Gimcrack Stakes. Magnier, though, was determined. So the year after that, he made Ferguson the owner of Rock of Gibraltar, which had won its first three races. Rock of Gibraltar won the Gimcrack easily and Magnier, waving a metaphorical two fingers at the racing authorities, watched Ferguson give the speech.

Magnier was largely making mischief, but he was also happy to do a favor for a friend, to give Ferguson a better experience of racing, and he benefited from the association of the horse with such a famous name. In addition, Ferguson did not get on well with the United chairman, Martin Edwards, and had a sense that football clubs were becoming good investments. Accordingly Magnier and his associate JP McManus bought shares in United. (The full story is explored by the journalist David Walsh here).

It turned out, though, that Rock of Gibraltar was a much better horse than anybody had realized, winning seven Group One races in a row. The stud fees would be worth tens of millions of pounds. Ferguson believed the verbal deal was that he could choose 50% of the prize money won by Rock of Gibraltar (about £800,000) or 50% of the stud fees, which ended up being worth tens of millions. He went for the latter. Magnier’s recollection was rather different: 5% of the prize money or one stud nomination a year.

Ferguson sued and, with his name on the ownership documents, probably would have won had it gone to trial. But then rumors started to spread about some of Ferguson’s financial dealings at United. Paid actors at United’s annual general meeting raised awkward points, then Magnier and McManus sent a list of 99 questions to the United board, which mysteriously found their way into the Daily Mail. United were highly embarrassed. Fans began to demonstrate against Magnier and McManus at race meetings. A settlement was reached, with Ferguson paid £2.5m to drop the action. But the damage was done.

Magnier and McManus had decided to sell their shares in United, and another shareholder was ready and waiting: Malcolm Glazer. Ferguson backed Glazer, who launched his leveraged buyout. Magnier and McManus sold up in 2005 for £260m, a profit of a little under £100m. Had they waited for Ratcliffe, who bought a similar stake in 2024, they would have received roughly £1bn more than that. For Ferguson, a threat had been dealt with.

The problem was that Glazer and his family would prove some of the worst club owners in English history. For 20 years, United have been addled by debt and have made consistently terrible footballing decisions. Ferguson’s team was good enough, and his personality big enough, that United won five league titles and a Champions League after the takeover, but once his genius had gone, there was nothing left.

A mismatched squad built up over seven flawed managerial appointments and a multiplicity of conflicting approaches will not readily be sorted out. Carrick is the latest victim of a crisis 21 years in the making. For the want of a horse a club was lost.
- This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US. Subscribe for free here.

articles.headline: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing
keyFacts: Anthropic warned that advanced artificial intelligence could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity in a filing ahead of its planned US stock market listing.
The AI company revealed losses of more than $80.7 billion alongside $112.4 billion in cash or equivalents and $16.3 billion in revenue for the first half of the year.
Anthropic will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT as the first true AI company to go public, though the share price, quantity, and listing date remain undisclosed.
body: - Published
Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.

The company behind AI chatbot Claude revealed losses of more than $80.7bn (Â£60.5bn) in the first half of the year, but said it had $112.4bn in cash or equivalents, and generated revenues of $16.3bn over the same period.
The number of shares to be released, their price range, and a date for the listing have not been disclosed.
Anthropic's valuation when it goes public has been expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which this summer was the biggest-ever stock listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion.

In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.

It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".
Anthropic will be the first true AI company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.
It said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT.
Anthropic, which was founded just five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five other co-founders, announced its intention to go public in June.

Its most significant rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit, saying it, too, intended to go public. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.

After the companies had decided on such plans, a wave of cyber-security and other types of technological breaches occurred involving their AI agents, or AI bots that are designed to operate somewhat autonomously.

Current and former staff of both companies also gained public attention with new warnings that AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect the whole of humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.
'Bold but sane'
In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.

In its financial filings, Anthropic detailed losses that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".
"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.
Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".

Tech companies have been heavily investing in costly AI infrastructure and tools, like data centres and the informational models that underly all AI technology, pouring more than $1tn into the efforts over the last year alone.

articles.headline: Iran’s ‘diabolical regime’ is rebuilding nuclear sites right under everyone’s noses, ex-general warns
keyFacts: Iran is accelerating construction and recovery efforts at multiple nuclear sites and its ballistic missile program.
Satellite networks and think tanks documented a surge of activity at the underground Pickaxe Mountain facility near Natanz.
Retired four-star Gen. Jack Keane told Fox News that the activity shows Iran has not abandoned its nuclear ambition.
body: Iran is accelerating the recovery efforts of their nuclear sites and ballistic missile program, with construction carrying on at multiple facilities, including Tehran’s infamous Pickaxe Mountain base.

Satellite networks and think tanks continue to document work across Iran’s nuclear and missile network, with a surge of activity recorded especially at the Pickaxe Mountain facility buried more than 300 feet underground near the Natanz atomic site.
The acceleration is evidence that Iran will not abandon its nuclear ambition despite ongoing peace talks with the US, retired four-star Gen. Jack Keane told Fox News.
“They certainly haven’t given up on it. It defines their regime,” Keane said. “We’re dealing with a diabolic regime”

“They recommitted themselves to the same goal they always have: to recover their nuclear program. To accelerate their ballistic missile program because they recognize what a threat that was for their opponents,” he added.

articles.headline: Mecca defence alliance members in Tehran to defuse Iran-US, Yemen tensions
keyFacts: Ministers and security officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye met with Iranian officials in Tehran to address regional security issues.
The diplomatic talks aim to defuse tensions between the United States and Iran amid threats of new US strikes.
Analysts suggest the meetings are primarily an attempt by the regional alliance to protect Saudi Arabia and encourage a compromise.
body: Tehran, Iran – Ministers and senior security officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye – the three nations that signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement – are in Tehran to discuss regional security issues amid threats of new US strikes on Iran.

Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, Pakistani military chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian and will discuss tensions with security chief Mohsen Rezaei.

The meetings are among the highest-profile dialogues held in Tehran in recent months. While there is still little information on what might be discussed, the meetings come amid a flurry of diplomatic activity to deal with a new escalation between the United States and Iran.

But analysts broadly believe the visit to Tehran by the three signatories of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, a regional defence alliance, will be enough to prevent a new outbreak in violence between the US and Iran.

“The Mecca pact’s 11th-hour visit to Tehran is an attempt to tip the balance in favour of those willing to compromise before the guns start blazing again,” said Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at the International Crisis Group.
“But unless they arrive with a credible formula to bridge the US-Iran divide, they may find themselves with little more than goodwill in a race against the clock.”

The talks are expected to address the waves of missile and drone attacks carried out by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, who are allied with Tehran, on Saudi Arabia, which supports Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

“I believe that parties to the Mecca agreement lack options of military engagement with the Houthis, but Riyadh is certainly asserting greater pressure for more, and its expectation of its partners has grown in parallel with the offensive from Yemen,” Ayesha Siddiqa, a senior research fellow in the Department of War Studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
But despite the collective security arrangement in the Mecca defence pact, Saudi Arabia’s allies Turkiye and Pakistan cannot “afford to commit troops on the ground” in Yemen, said Siddiqa.

The latest diplomatic push is likely linked to visits by Pakistani army chief Asim Munir to Saudi Arabia and Iran last week, Siddiqa said, and coincides with Islamabad’s restrictions on overland border trade with Tehran amid the US blockade on Iran.
Iranian authorities have said they favoured “security originating from within the region” as they prepared for the meetings.

Umer Karim, who researches Saudi foreign policy and its implications for regional security, said the Tehran meetings are unlikely to reduce the risk of a renewed war between Iran and the US, which would likely lead to more regional turmoil.
“Therefore, these talks perhaps are more concerned about the security of Saudi Arabia and involve an attempt by Turkiye and Pakistan to compel Iran to reach a compromise,” he told Al Jazeera.

US President Donald Trump is said to be considering new attacks to break the diplomatic deadlock with Iran, which has refused to agree to any peace agreement with Washington unless several of its demands are met.

The US and regional powers want international shipping and transit through the Strait of Hormuz to resume without impediments or attacks. Washington also wants to rein in Tehran’s nuclear programme and bring in international inspectors to assess Iran’s highly enriched uranium. Israel says it wants to overthrow the Islamic Republic.

Tehran wants to lift the US naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports, which has halted crude oil exports and disrupted most trade, and return to a memorandum of understanding agreed between the two countries in June.

The US has refused this, with President Trump saying he is left with a choice to “finish the job” by launching major strikes on Iran’s civilian infrastructure. This could prompt Iran to lash out at its neighbours, as it did earlier in the war with strikes on US bases in Arab states and infrastructure.

Meanwhile, the US Department of State issued an October 21 order for nonemergency US government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia for their safety’s sake, given the Houthi threat.

As talks involving Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye continue in Iran, analysts say these Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signatories will likely try to minimise the impact on Saudi Arabia if war does break out again.

“However, since little has changed from an Iranian strategic calculus and the actors involved don’t have the kind of leverage needed to affect Iran’s strategic thinking, these negotiations are going to yield little,” Karim said.

articles.headline: How the Rays fixed Freddy Peralta: The changes that propelled him back to ace form after ugly Mets stint
keyFacts: Right-hander Freddy Peralta will start Game 3 of the World Series for the Tampa Bay Rays after being acquired from the New York Mets at the trade deadline.
The Rays fixed Peralta by changing his delivery to pitch exclusively from the stretch, raising his arm angle, and adding extension toward the plate.
Tampa also increased Peralta's changeup usage and benefited from the team's strong defensive support behind him.
body: When the Tampa Bay Rays return home Monday for the first World Series game at Tropicana Field since 2008, they will give the ball to one of their shortest-tenured players. Right-hander Freddy Peralta, acquired from the New York Mets at the trade deadline, will start Game 3. It will be his first start since his stellar performance in Game 6 of the ALCS, which .

"It feels so good because the way that we've been working on the little things in general," Peralta said after Game 6. "Everybody, not only the pitching coach and all that, I mean everybody from the trainers, people that helped me to feel better with the massage and all that, it's been amazing. Great communication. They've been awesome with me. They've been giving the best of themselves to make me feel good on the field every day."

A year ago, Peralta led the league with 17 wins and finished fifth in the NL Cy Young voting with the Milwaukee Brewers, the team he will face as . As they tend to do, the Brewers traded Peralta in the offseason, a year before he was scheduled to hit free agency. Peralta went to the Mets, disappointed, was traded to the Rays at the deadline, and has since surged.

"His three months or four months in New York probably didn't go the way he wanted or the way he performed his first five years (in the league)," Rays manager Kevin Cash said before the World Series. "... I give Freddy a lot of credit for being a good pitcher and being vulnerable enough to say, 'I wasn't comfortable doing some things and I want to get back to my strengths.' He guided that through the entire two months he's been with us, and he took off in September and has continued to take off in October."

The Rays are as good as any team at taking a player, accentuating his strengths, and getting the best out of him. Peralta is no different. This isn't a case of a good pitcher having a few rough months and then getting his season on track. The Rays took Peralta into the lab and made several important changes that have led to this success.
Here's how Tampa fixed Peralta in their brief time with him after the trade deadline.
Mechanical changes

It starts with the delivery and introducing a common trait for Rays pitchers. They take away the full windup and have the pitcher pitch exclusively from the stretch. Ace Drew Rasmussen is the best example of this. Peralta might be the second best. As soon as the Rays got their hands on Peralta, they took away his windup and got him to pitch from the stretch to simplify things.
Here's how it looked before and after the change. This is the first pitch of Peralta's final start with the Mets, and the first pitch of his first start with the Rays (GIFs synced at release):

Pitching from the stretch improved many things for Peralta, including his command. Location+ is a metric that grades pitch locations not just on whether they're on the edges of the zone, but whether the pitcher puts that pitch in the right part of the zone. Is that four-seamer at the top of the zone? Is the changeup down and away? You won't score well for hanging a slider just because it's a strike.

Peralta posted a solid 104 Location+ with the Mets, which is comfortably above the 100 MLB average. With the Rays, it jumped to 111, which is better than his 2025 rate (108 Location+) and would have been one of the highest marks in the game for the full season. Peralta went from good location with the Mets to great location with the Rays, thanks in part to his new delivery.

The Rays also helped Peralta raise his arm angle a bit, something that is very difficult to do in-season and an adjustment pitchers usually work on in the offseason or Spring Training. He also added extension and drive toward the plate, meaning he's getting further down the mound and releasing the ball closer to the hitter.

With the added extension and higher arm angle came more velocity and more vertical break on the fastball, which is "life" up in the zone. The Rays took away his windup, but they did not create an entirely new Peralta. They simply got him back to the 2025 version of himself, and it all starts with the delivery. Pitching from the stretch has allowed him to execute at a much higher level.

"When I got here, when I sat here with (pitching coach) Kyle (Snyder) and (bullpen coach Jorge Moncada) and Cash, they told me, 'You're gonna do what you want to do here, and we are going to help you to do it. And we know what you need to do to make those adjustments,'" Peralta told MLB.com in September. "We just put everything on the table. I just followed all the instructions, and it's what I am right now."
Pitch selection

In addition to the mechanical changes, the Rays also tweaked Peralta's pitch mix, specifically getting him to use his changeup more often. This is a Rays staple. Their pitchers threw an MLB-leading 20.6% changeups in 2026. The next team, the San Diego Padres, threw only 16.3% changeups. The gap between No. 1 and No. 2 was the same as the gap between No. 2 and No. 13.

Peralta's changeup usage jumped from an already healthy 20.8% with the Mets to 29.7% with the Rays. Against right-handed batters specifically, it jumped from 15.8% to 22.2%. Same-side changeups are another Rays specialty. Usually, you throw changeups to hitters on the other side of the plate, but not Tampa. They love same-side changeups and Peralta has bought in.

Between the combination of swings and misses and weak contact, the changeup is Peralta's best-performing pitch, so the Rays have him throwing it more often. "Throw your best pitch more" is a pretty simple concept, but not always something pitchers and teams will adhere to. The Rays got Peralta to pull back on everything else, throw more changeups, and the results have followed.

"We were trying to make adjustments," Peralta said Saturday about his time with the Mets. "We knew, we understood, and we spoke with each other about it. I remember that we were doing the right thing because we were preparing in the right way, but we couldn't do what we were supposed to do."
How much has Peralta improved, really?

There are some elements of Peralta's performance with Tampa that likely would not continue across a full 162-game season. That isn't to say he's been lucky -- I hate that term -- but baseball is a game of ebbs and flows, and right now Peralta is riding a wave in which the outcomes have gone in his direction. Over time, they would likely even out, but they haven't yet.
Here are some more numbers:

Expected ERA (xERA) estimates a pitcher's ERA and factors in contact quality allowed (exit velocity, etc.), and it views Peralta as basically the same pitcher with the Rays as he was with the Mets. Despite similar contact allowed, he's given up way fewer hits on balls in play (BABIP) and fewer home runs on fly balls (HR/FB%). By comparison, Peralta had a .243 BABIP and 10.4 HR/FB% in 2025.

You would expect Peralta to have a lower BABIP with the Rays than with the Mets for two reasons. One, the Mets were a poor defensive team this season. It was appaulingly bad at times. The Rays rate as an above-average defensive team, especially in the outfield. Peralta has a low BABIP with the Rays in part thanks to his teammates, who are great at catching the baseball.

"That's a huge part, man," Peralta said about Tampa's defense Saturday. "Sometimes I face hitters that I understand in the moment that I have to -- OK, I tell myself, just whatever I'm going to throw, just put it in the zone. Just looking for the hitter to hit the ball because I know and trust all the guys I have behind me, and it's been working pretty well. I just trust them."

The HR/FB% rate is more difficult to explain. Tropicana Field is more home run-friendly than Citi Field, per Statcast's park factors, plus Peralta made road starts at Coors Field, Citizens Bank Park, and Sutter Health Park in Sacramento with the Rays. He pitched in some home run-happy parks yet gave up fewer homers. Peralta may have caught some breaks in the home run department.

Ultimately, none of this matters right now. It has no bearing on how Peralta will perform in Game 3 or a potential Game 7. His BABIP and HR/FB% rate are not guaranteed to regress back to his true talent level this week. They were low during his stint with the Rays, yes, but it happened and it helped Tampa win games. Now he and the Rays just need to continue for another start or two.

"I love that kid, man, I just do," Brewers manager Pat Murphy said about Peralta before that World Series. "If you're around him every day, like this kid is just joyful. It's just a beautiful spirit that comes to do his job. He doesn't look at himself as better than others. He's just a great teammate. If you can't be around him for a while and not feel warm ... Just a matter of time before Freddy broke through because he was great for us for so many years."

articles.headline: Anthropic officially files for its public debut
keyFacts: Anthropic filed for an initial public offering on Monday, according to the firm's latest SEC filing.
Anthropic recorded revenue of $16.3 billion and a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half of 2026.
Anthropic has not yet disclosed its proposed share price or how much it hopes to raise.
body: After weeks of leaked S-1s, Anthropic finally filed for an initial public offering on Monday, setting the stage for one of the most closely watched public debuts in modern U.S. history.

Anthropic, which plans to list under the ticker “ANT,” recorded revenue of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year, according to the firm’s latest SEC filing.

That revenue came off the back of an operating loss of $693 million, an improvement from the $2.1 billion in operating losses that Anthropic recorded in the first half of 2025. Anthropic’s net loss, however, hit $80.7 billion, which was largely driven by noncash accounting adjustments tied to convertible debt. The company says it “may not achieve or sustain profitability in the future.”

The filing also provided more color on the scale of Anthropic’s enterprise business. As of the end of September, Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers spending $100,000 or more annually; 1,900 customers spending $1 million or more; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more.

As previously reported, Anthropic’s governance structure will enable Anthropic’s seven co-founders to maintain control once the company goes public. Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah will make up the “Founder LLC,” which will collectively control 50.1% of shareholder voting power — a move Anthropic says is designed to preserve the company’s AI safety mission, per the filing.
Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, established in 2023 to ensure the company pursues its public benefit mission, will have the authority to appoint most of the company’s board.

The governance structure is controversial because it means voting power is not proportional to the founders’ economic ownership, and therefore public shareholders will have little practical control over a company building technology that, by its own admission, poses “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it hopes to raise nor its proposed share price.

articles.headline: Ireland prop Furlong cited over alleged groin grab
keyFacts: Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong has been cited for an alleged groin grab during Leinster's win over Munster.
Munster back row Gavin Coombes raised the allegation during the match, though video evidence was not found at the time.
The United Rugby Championship stated that arrangements for the disciplinary process are currently in progress.
body: - Published
Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong has been cited over an alleged groin grab in Leinster's United Rugby Championship win over Munster on Saturday.

Munster back row Gavin Coombes raised the allegation against an unnamed Leinster player with match referee Andrew Brace in the closing stages of the first half at the Aviva Stadium, but television match official (TMO) Colin Stanley could not find any video evidence at the time.

However, experienced front row Furlong has now been cited over an act of foul play under Law 9.27, which says a "a player must not do anything that is against the spirit of good sportsmanship including but not limited to grabbing, twisting or squeezing the genitals".
A statement from the URC said "arrangements for the disciplinary process are currently in progress and will be announced in due course".

If found guilty of the offence, the 33-year-old would be in danger of missing Ireland's Nations Championship matches with Argentina, Fiji and South Africa in Dublin, as well as the finals weekend in London.
In October 2025, South Africa front-rower Jan-Hendrik Wessels received a nine-match suspension for grabbing Josh Murphy's genitals in the Bulls' URC win over Connacht.

For that incident, Wessels was handed a 12-week suspension - the shortest ban under World Rugby rules for such an offence - that was reduced by three weeks due to his "good conduct prior to and at the hearing and good record".
If similar action was taken against Furlong, he would potentially miss Leinster's Investec Champions Cup Pool match with Sale, as well as the festive inter-provincial derbies with Ulster and Munster.
Speaking after the 24-18 defeat at the Aviva Stadium, Munster head coach Clayton McMillan said he would "back our players 100% that if they make an allegation like that".
Leinster head coach Leo Cullen said he did not see the incident, which occurred in the 37th minute when Munster were leading, but acknowledged it was a "serious matter".

articles.headline: Australian judge rejects prisoner's human rights challenge to Vegemite ban
keyFacts: An Australian judge rejected a life-sentenced prisoner's human rights challenge against a state prison ban on Vegemite.
Inmate Andre McKechnie argued that withholding Vegemite breached his right to enjoy his culture as an Australian.
Justice Claire Harris ruled the ban was justified after prison officials testified Vegemite could hinder drug dogs and help brew alcohol.
body: Australian judge rejects prisoner's human rights challenge to Vegemite ban

MELBOURNE, Australia — A prisoner on Monday lost his challenge to an Australian state's ban on inmates eating Vegemite after he argued in court that withholding the polarizing yeast-based spread breached his human right to "enjoy his culture as an Australian."
Andre McKechnie, 55, who is serving a life sentence for murder, took his battle for the salty, sticky, black-brown byproduct of brewing beer to the Supreme Court of the state of Victoria last year.

He had argued being refused Vegemite denied him his right under the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act to "enjoy his culture as an Australian in the community with other persons of Australian background," court documents showed.
Justice Claire Harris accepted prison authorities' refusal to allow McKechnie Vegemite "limited his cultural rights" under the charter.
But she found the ban was justified in meeting authorities' goals of removing illicit drugs and alcohol from the prison system.
"The limitation on Mr. McKechnie's ability to enjoy Vegemite in community with other persons of Australian background is primarily that he is a prisoner," Harris wrote in her 47-page judgment.
Prison officials testify Vegemite could impair drug sniffer dogs and be used to make alcohol

Prison officials testified at a trial in July that Vegemite had been banned throughout the state's 12 prisons for the past 20 years because it could potentially impair sniffer dogs' ability to detect narcotics and could be used to brew alcohol because of its yeast content.

McKechnie, who represented himself in court by video link from maximum security Barwon Prison west of Melbourne, argued that the fact that neighboring New South Wales state did not ban Vegemite from its prisons was evidence that there were "less restrictive means reasonably available" to achieve such drug and alcohol outcomes.

Most Australians revere Vegemite as an unfairly maligned culinary icon, and more than 80% of Australian households are estimated to have a jar in their pantries. Vegemite is typically considered an acquired taste at best by those who weren't raised on it.
The last U.S. president to visit Australia, Barack Obama, once said: "It's horrible."
Prisoner argues Vegemite ban contributed to vitamin deficiency
McKechnie had initially testified that the lack of Vegemite had contributed to his thiamine deficiency.
He said both Vegemite and pork were sources of thiamine, also known as vitamin B1. As a Jew who observed kosher law, he told the court he couldn't eat pork either and took daily doses of the vitamin.
Vegemite has long been marketed as a source of B vitamins thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3) and folate (B9) which are promoted as healthy additions to the diets of growing children.
But McKechnie dropped the thiamine issue as "not important," after lawyers for the prison authorities objected to his evidence.
Prisoner said Vegemite ban left him feeling 'deprived, sad and disconnected'
McKechnie said not eating Vegemite made him feel "deprived of being able to practice my Australian culture, sad and disconnected from my family and community."

The judge responded that "it is difficult to accept that the inability to consume Vegemite, rather than the fact of his imprisonment, is a material cause of his sadness and disconnection from his family and community."
McKechnie cited an article published in the food studies journal "Gastronomica" in 2003 that said, "Vegemite may be the best predictor of national identity of any food in the world."
The article, based on research by Australia's Queensland University in 1995, found that a "taste for the spread strongly correlates with early exposure and to Australian birth and ancestry."
McKechnie also referred to the Australian Olympic Committee overturning an Chinese import ban on Vegemite ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing.
He cited Australian band Men at Work's 1980s international hit "Down Under" that mentions a "Vegemite sandwich."

On the effectiveness of smearing contraband with Vegemite, McKechnie cited a Melbourne newspaper article from 2017 that reported a man's unsuccessful attempt to use the odor of the spread to conceal illicit drugs that he attempted to smuggle into a music festival in Victoria. The attempt was thwarted by police sniffer dogs.
Judge rejects evidence that Vegemite doesn't interfere with drug sniffer dogs
The judge upheld prison authorities' argument that McKechnie had failed to provide any proper foundations for his opinion that Vegemite does not interfere with drug sniffer dogs.
McKechnie also argued that Vegemite contained "no live yeast" and that any piece of fruit would be more useful in making alcohol than the spread.
A state prison department manager, Kevin White, cited publicly available research that said Vegemite helped home-brewed beer ferment more quickly.
Vegemite's owner, Bega Group, did not respond to a request for comment on Monday.

articles.headline: Careers on the line for Australia in deciding South Africa Test?
keyFacts: Australia and South Africa meet in a third Test series-decider at Cape Town with the series locked at 1-1.
Australia's Marnus Labuschagne faces pressure to save his spot, while Steve Smith faces a late fitness test for a neck problem.
The match will be broadcast live on Sky Sports Cricket and Sky Sports Main Event starting Tuesday.
body: South Africa meet Australia in third Test series-decider at Cape Town with careers on the line for tourists

Australia's Marnus Labuschagne may have one innings to save his skin as poor run continues in South Africa; Steve Smith faces late fitness test; series locked at 1-1 after South Africa's innings victory in Gqeberha; watch live on Sky Sports Cricket from 7.30am, Tuesday
Monday 26 October 2026 13:17, UK
Australia are about to play a Test match in Cape Town for the first time since the ball-tampering scandal back in 2018 that paused a number of their cricketers' careers.
Should they lose to South Africa this week in the series decider, live on Sky Sports Cricket, a number of careers could be ended.
Having been humbled by an innings and 31 runs in Gqeberha last time out, a game in which they were torpedoed for 99 in the first innings, the Baggy Greens need a response.

If that does not come, the reaction from the Australian media could be more abrasive than the piece of sandpaper Cameron Bancroft aimed to conceal down his trousers eight years ago.
The batting has been creaking for a while.

In the 4-1 Ashes thrashing of England last winter, it was held together by Travis Head, Steve Smith and Alex Carey as others toiled, while in South Africa so far the tourists have managed only three individual fifty-plus scores - one for Head and two for Matt Renshaw.
Without Head in Durban, things would have been even grislier. His second-innings 121 was 81 more runs than the next highest score by an Aussie in the game.

Even the great Smith - who received a ban for the role he played as skipper in 'Sandpapergate' in 2018, along with Bancroft and David Warner - has stuttered: three innings' in the 20s and a knock of three.
He was hampered by a neck problem in Gqeberha and faces a late fitness Test ahead of the winner-takes-all Cape Town finale.
If he fails that, it could aid Marnus Labuschagne's hopes of staying in the side.
Labuschagne and selector Bailey under big pressure?

Former Australia captain Ricky Ponting had branded Labuschagne's spot as "untenable" after a lean return at home to Bangladesh left him without a Test century in 43 innings, stretching back to the 2023 Ashes in England. That has now extended to 47 innings.
Labuschagne has had no trouble starting in South Africa, the country of his birth - reaching the 30s in three of his four outings. But he has not kicked on.

Pinned lbw. Sliced loosely to cover. Brilliantly caught by Simon Harmer at gully. And then a criminal dismissal as he inexplicably holed out to long-on in the second innings of the second Test, a game Australia were trying to save.
If he misses out this week, it could be curtains. If he plays and fails, it could be a similar story. If Australia fail as a team, perhaps pressure will mount on head selector George Bailey?

Former skipper Steve Waugh said before the Ashes that Bailey has previously shown a lack of "appetite" to make the big calls, while the selection of the now-jettisoned Nic Maddinson for the South Africa tour was panned at the time by Matthew Hayden.
Maddinson ditching after recall highlights Australia's issues
Maddinson, 34, had not played a first-class game since March 2025 due to a testicular cancer diagnosis and averaged 6.75 from his first three Tests back in 2016.
Hayden accused selectors of "disrespecting first-class cricket" and "promoting the greatest pile of mediocrity that we've seen in a generation of cricket."

Maddinson has not been as good as mediocre in this series, with his average a paltry 14 after amassing only 56 runs from four knocks - 48 of which came in one innings to punctuate a 33-ball duck, a four-ball duck and a 10-ball eight.
He has since been released from the squad, with Renshaw poised to open alongside Head in Cape Town.
Considering what he went through health-wise, people were rooting for Maddinson to perform but he hasn't. It raises the question over whether a younger player should have been given a go instead.
Ollie Davies, Sam Konstas and Campbell Kellaway were options. Nathan McSweeney, too.

The problem Australia have is that unlike in previous eras when they had players averaging north of 40 and banging out domestic runs - often in English county cricket as well as at home - waiting in the wings, they don't now.
All of the prospects mentioned above average mid-30s or lower in first-class cricket.
Will Bavuma extend excellent record as captain?
South Africa, by contrast, have a pretty much guaranteed source of runs in captain Temba Bavuma, whose brilliant 179 from 334 balls in Gqeberha means he is averaging 49.95 across his last 28 Tests.
His nuggety ton last time out was scored after he came in at 12-2.
He was at the other end as the Proteas slumped to 110-6 before pushing them to 425-9 and was ultimately left to celebrate a 12th win in 14 Tests as skipper.
This feels like a great chance to make that 13 from 15 unless Australia are able to pull something out of the bag in Cape Town.
Unlike in 2018, something within the rules this time.
